utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Everyone is here from last Friday, so it is not necessary to have the appearances apart from the Prosecution. Mr. Mundis, could you please present your colleague to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We're accompanied today by Mr. Pieter Kruger, one of the trial attorneys on this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm having a look at Defence counsel. Everyone was present on Friday. No one new is here. I'd like to greet everyone present in the courtroom; the accused, Defence counsel, as well as the members of the Prosecution. But I believe that Ms. Nozica would like to introduce her co-counsel to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. I would just like to say that we now have Mr. Peter Murphy as co-counsel, which was not the case on Friday. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will be continuing with our work today. We have a new witness. I know that the Prosecution will soon be taking the floor, but before I give the floor to the Prosecution, there two oral decisions I would like to render that concerns the procedure we will be following. The first decision has to do with the disclosure of Defence exhibits in the course of the cross-examination. The Judges have decided that Defence counsel shall disclose to the Prosecution the documents that they intend to tender immediately prior to the beginning of the cross-examination. On the other hand, 24 hours earlier, the Registrar shall be provided with the documents so that they can be registered in accordance with the e-court procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What should be pointed out is that these documents will be disclosed before the beginning of the cross-examination, but also just after the end of the examination-in-chief. That means that if the examination-in-chief is concluded at 1500 hours, at 1500 hours and one second Defence counsel shall disclose the documents. But if the examination-in-chief is concluded at 1900 hours, in that case the Defence shall disclose the documents at 1900 hours and one second. The cross-examination shall then commence on the following day. That is my first -- that is the first decision. Now, the second oral decision that I'd like to inform you of concerns how Defence counsel shall proceed in the course of cross-examination, how they shall proceed with their interrogation. Yesterday --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: On Friday, that is, interpreter's correction,

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- some members of the Defence didn't have sufficient time to put the questions they wanted to put to the witness. Given that, we realise that if there is no agreement reached by the Defence counsel, each member of the Defence should have one-sixth of the allocated time. Each member of the Defence counsel shall have a sixth of the time allocated to the Prosecution unless members of the Defence counsel have reached an agreement according to which some members will put questions on behalf of the others. But failing such an agreement, each member of the Defence counsel shall have a sixth of the time allocated to the Prosecution. If the Prosecution has two hours for its examination-in-chief, each member of the Defence counsel shall be allocated 20 minutes. If the Prosecution takes three hours for its examination-in-chief, each member of the Defence counsel shall have 30 minutes. If the Prosecution takes four hours - and that's how long they believe they will need for today's witness - in that case, each member of the Defence counsel will have 40 minutes for their cross-examination. In addition, on each occasion we will decide on the order of appearances for Defence counsel. On Friday, Mr. Karnavas commenced with the cross-examination. Today, Ms. Nozica will commence, and then everyone will take their turn. The next time we'll start with Mr. Kovacic, and so on. So you will take turns to commence your cross-examination and thus we won't always have the same member of Defence counsel asking the most important questions. So you will take turns to be in front position when cross-examining a witness. This is the procedure that we have decided on. I know that there is something that Mr. Mundis would like to say with regard to next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. In order to do that, if we could, we would ask to go into private session for just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Registrar, could we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are back in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now that we're in open session, I give you the floor, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, very briefly with regard to this decision according to which we are obliged to disclose our documents that we have prepared for our cross-examination immediately after the end of the examination-in-chief. With regard to this decision, could you excuse me if I fail to comply with that decision today, because I wasn't prepared for it? I don't have many assistants. They are involved in other matters today, so I don't think I'm in a position to comply with your decision today. And my assistants are only putting these documents into electronic form, so I don't know whether I'll be in a position to finish with this today. That will be the case before the cross-examination, but I don't know whether I'll be able to comply with your decision today. And then there is another decision of yours which is a lot more important and that concerns allocating a sixth of the Prosecution's time to each member of the Defence counsel. This is a decision I'd like to know something more about. Will we also have a written decision that will be provided to us? I'm asking about this so as I know how to deal with the possibility of an appeal, an interlocutory appeal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the oral decision doesn't appear very clear to you, we will also provide you with a written decision if you so wish. I don't think it's necessary because it just concerns the procedure that will be followed, and for an interlocutory appeal it's also necessary for such an appeal to be certified. I'd like to remind you of this fact. Let's avoid wasting time, because if there are six of you who take the floor on each occasion that an issue is raised, we'll have to spend an hour on the matter and we will be losing that time that could have been used for a witness. Mr. Jonjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. There is one thing I'm not quite clear about. When we prepare for the cross-examination of a witness, we'll prepare certain documents, and depending on the number of facts we are aware of -- well, our preparation depends on the facts we are aware of. So the documents we have prepared for today are documents we can provide the Prosecution with as of tomorrow. It's too late to do that today. But what happens when, in the course of the examination-in-chief, the witness says something that we hadn't expected? Perhaps we have certain documents, but we can't prepare these documents by the time the cross-examination -- by the time the examination-in-chief has been concluded. So could you please clarify that matter for us. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In -- if a witness raises an issue in the course of the examination-in-chief, an issue that you hadn't expected when compiling your list of documents, well, this is something that can happen, but in such a case you will always have the possibility of presenting a document that isn't on the list. You should, in that case, say that the witness addressed an issue and that as a result it's necessary for you to file a certain document. This is a case that can arise, but it's not something that will happen all the time. If there are no further issues to discuss, we will call the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I do have one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just to be on the record, Your Honour. I understand your rulings of one-sixth. If and when the time comes where I don't believe I can adequately represent my client as a result of this, I will have to withdraw from the case and I will do so immediately. I will not be part of a trial where I cannot properly represent my client because of some rule that's fast and hard with this calculation. The Prosecution took more time than it indicated because they have their case. We took less than we were allotted because it wasn't necessary. I don't think that we can have this rule. I also think that when you look at the indictment, the indictment is in a particular order because the person who is at the top, and the second person and the third person, it's in the order of importance. So you don't have the person at the bottom who is the most responsible. You have a joint criminal enterprise, and the way it's done is in a pyramid fashion. So I'm just putting the Court on notice, and I want a very clear record, that if and when the time comes because of a completion strategy that somebody in New York has decided to place on us that I'm unable to properly represent my client, I cannot part of a process where I cannot ethically follow my own code of ethics. And I appreciate and I will abide by the Court's orders, but at the same time I cannot, you know, proceed if I cannot represent my client. He's at the top of the list. There's a period of three or four years. The Prosecution spent eight years on this case, and I don't think it's fair, I do not think it's fair to say to me that you have one-sixth of the time the Prosecution has to do your case when it's virtually impossible to predict. So I just put the Court on notice. I understand you have a difficult task, Your Honours. I truly understand that. But I don't think you should allow political pressure from New York to prevent you from allowing the Defence to take their necessary time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise for taking the floor again. I'll try to be as brief as possible, but there is one other thing I have to add. Last week we had two witnesses. Initially, the rules were flexible, but you established certain principles. I believe that those two witnesses that we heard last week demonstrated that Defence counsel abided by the principle established by you. In both cases, we didn't exceed the amount of time allocated to the Prosecution as far as the pace or the speed of proceedings are concerned. And I'm quite aware of the fact that, as the Presiding Judge, you have to take time constraints into consideration, you have to take the completion strategy into consideration. I'm quite aware of all these factors, but that shouldn't be done to the detriment of the rights of the accused. My client isn't one-sixth of the accused. He's an individual. He's the third person accused in this case. He could have been accused individually or with some of the accused or with 19 of them. If Tudjman, Susak, and Bobetko, Boban and others hadn't died - and they are mentioned in the introduction to this indictment - then these deceased would also have been included in the indictment. Would that have meant that we would have been allocated only one-fifteenth of the time allocated to the Prosecution? I don't think so. Your Honours, we are abiding by your guidelines. Let's continue abiding by your guidelines. But not each member of Defence counsel has the same Defence strategy, so we don't have the possibility to reach agreement on how the cross-examination should be conducted. We had a slight problem when last hearing was held, but we all realised that it was because it was Friday, the witness was an elderly man, there was a misunderstanding between Defence counsel and the Chamber. We all wanted the witness to go home on Friday, and as a result, my colleagues were more cooperative than they would have been. It would have been more natural for the witness to stay on for one more day. But that doesn't matter. I don't think any harm was done. But if we insist on the procedure you have mentioned, I don't know how we will manage to proceed. There is one other matter I would like to mention. As you requested, the Prosecution -- or your decision of the 30th of November has not been respected, your decision that would make it clearer to us to know what the subject of someone's testimony will be. So we're still trying to find our way in the Prosecution's announcements. But in this case, in this particular case, in the case of the witness we are supposed to be hearing today, the Prosecution has mentioned a number of -- a significant number of paragraphs. He's referred to 90 per cent of the indictment, I would say. However, in the submission dated the 19th of January, the Prosecution also mentioned that that witness was -- was relevant only for my client. So the paragraphs are referred to in the indictment, but only my client is concerned. Why am I mentioning this? This is something that makes it impossible for us to divide the work, to decide who will discuss certain issues, provided that the witness mentions certain issues that are indicated. And now in the paragraphs provided by the Prosecution, the Prosecution refers to paragraphs in the indictment - let's say paragraph 17 and paragraph 39 - and in those two paragraphs, 17 and 39, you will find the names of all six accused. The Prosecution says that this witness only relates to my client, though, Your Honours. It's not just that I'm confused now and I don't know how to prepare myself, even if it only concerns me or if this only concerns my client, but if six Defence lawyers sit down, which we did on Sunday afternoon in my office, and analyse these paragraphs and these names, well, believe me, it's not necessary to tell you all of the theories that we could have thought of and all of the matters we could have expected. So we could only agree to disagree. We couldn't reach any agreements. It's not that we -- we didn't fail to reach an agreement because our Defence strategy was different. In this case we couldn't reach an agreement because we couldn't understand what the Prosecution actually wanted to do. We didn't understand the Prosecution's objectives. And let me conclude, Your Honours. In this particular case, we couldn't reach an agreement because your order dated the 30th of November was not abided by. That was the first order issued by the Chamber, and the Prosecution was quite clearly instructed as to how they should present all the documents and witnesses that they were referring to. And the Prosecution has failed to comply with that order to date. I believe that you had to grant them extra time. But until they comply with your order, we'll be in a state of confusion. I think you extended that deadline up until September. But please, don't force us to have only one-sixth of the time, at least not until September if we are not in a position to know whether a given witness will really be testifying only with regard to my client or with regard to all six accused. Are we referring to a joint criminal enterprise or not? I do not know. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, in relation to what you just said, I personally fully agree with that, and I have no objections to what you just said. Indeed, what you said now, had this ruling dated the 30th of November been complied with, then we would have known in relation to witnesses who testified last week precisely what the Prosecution intends to show through that witness. You'll remember that in that order we asked the Prosecution to tell us clearly what paragraphs of the -- what paragraphs of the indictment pertain to a particular witness. We asked the Prosecution to quote from their pre-trial briefs and the indictment in relation to each individual witness. In addition to that, we also asked that the Prosecution tell us to which of the accused is the testimony of a certain witness going to relate. The Prosecutor told us that they are unable to do that, especially bearing in mind the voluminous of their filings. Then we adopted a new order, asking that the Prosecution provide a document to us in compliance with our November order for each individual witness, starting in September. You told us that you got together in order to discuss this problem. That was a good idea, because it is only through such meetings and discussions that you are able to determine which Defence team is interested in a particular witness. Mr. Karnavas told us that, in view of the hierarchy of responsibility, the first accused is at the top of the list and the last accused is at the bottom of the list. This is Mr. Karnavas's interpretation and yours as well. Depending on that -- or, rather, on the basis of that, you believe you should be allocated more time than other Defence teams. The Trial Chamber told you that you have to agree among yourselves. But, however, if you are unable to agree among yourselves, then we will have to issue some kind of a ruling. So only failing your agreement will this mechanism kick in where everybody will have one-sixth of the time. So the examination may concern such issues as water supply, was there sufficient water supply, was there lack thereof, and so on. These are factual issues. We are not getting into individual criminal responsibility yet. Once we get to such witnesses, however, it is clear that the time would not be allocated in the same way. For example, when we have to establish how was somebody killed, then the situation will be different. For example, if somebody's primarily interested in a certain witness, then that Defence team should lead that cross-examination or use up the majority of the time allotted to Defence, and then the rest of Defence counsel will share among them the remaining time. However, I see that you have not been able to agree among yourselves on this. We saw with the Prosecution that last week we spent a lot of time discussing the issue of water supply. This is mentioned in the following paragraphs of the indictment: 113, and 114. And a lot of time was used up on that. If the Prosecution continues wasting time like this, I will interrupt them. I will point this out to them. So if we once again have a situation where questions that do not seem relevant or useful to us are being put, then we will have to intervene. Had we received this document, as Defence pointed out, the document that we requested, then we would know where things are headed. As it is, it is impossible to know where we are headed. The Judges and Defence wish to know what is the purpose of the examination-in-chief. I'm bringing up this example with water supply as just one of examples. This is our ruling. If you wish to appeal it, then we will issue this ruling in writing as well and, if necessary, the Appeals Chamber will decide on this. However, if you fail to agree among yourselves, it is impossible for us to give you, all of you, the same amount of time as the Prosecution. It is impossible. So at some point we have to make an executive decision on this. That's all I have to tell you on this issue. Your words and your arguments were not useful in the sense that they did not point to a solution to this problem. We have to work on the basis of the indictment and pre-trial briefs. The mistake of the Prosecution is as follows: You do not have in your pre-trial brief any footnotes related to documents that you intend to introduce into evidence. It would have been much easier had we received complete footnotes, because then we would have been able to see where you headed. For example, the issue of water is mentioned in some of the documents but you didn't point that out in footnotes and this is why we find ourselves in this situation, both the Chamber and the Defence. However, I hope that as the time passes, you will be much more efficient so that we will be able to tailor both examination-in-chief and cross-examination to the existing circumstances. The beginning stage of every trial is usually the most difficult one, but as the time passes, things get easier. They improve. So there's always some time needed for warm-up, but we need to conclude this stage. This is the second week of warm-up, and I think it needs to be brought to an end. Yes. Please go ahead, Mr. Kovacic. That's it, Mr. Kovacic. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, very briefly to respond to a couple of points that have been made in the last 40 minutes. In terms of the filings and the time estimates and the references to particular accused, what the Prosecution has consistently said in all of our filings is all of this information is, by necessity, based on an ongoing assessment - you can use the word "guesstimate," if you like - which are always subject to change. For example, last week during the second witness, I indicated at the beginning that I added visual references to paragraphs and counts of the indictment. Frankly, there is some substantial amount of subjectivity in listening and reading a particular paragraph and saying, "I think this paragraph and this paragraph are the ones that it most directly relates to," and when the witness comes, when you talk to the witness, you might look at the indictment again and say, I think really, in fairness, it also relates to paragraph so-and-so and paragraph so-and-so. It is in the nature of these filings, and that's why -- one of the reasons why the Prosecution is concerned about these various filings is that they not be taken as written in stone. I can -- I can assure you that if we make predictions as to witnesses that will come from a year from now, I assure you a number of those predictions will be wrong. We will find out there are new exhibits, we will find out there are things they tell us when they come to The Hague that are different. I assure you any filing that we make today or a week from now or a month from now or in September will be subject to ongoing change and revision. That is the nature -- that is simply the nature of the process. As to the hierarchy in listing of the indictment, Your Honour, there is no particular magic in that. It's fair to say that there is some very, very general reference or listing in terms of Mr. Prlic was the president, Mr. Stojic was the minister of defence. There was some -- you had to choose someone. I suppose we could have simply drawn names out of a hat and decided which accused to list first but let's not ascribe too much importance to that. I don't think it should be overstated that the order listed in the indictment is of some particular or significant importance. They are -- all six are charged, all six are accused in the indictment. As to the paragraphs, the indictment, Your Honour, again as to water. I'll be very, very brief, but it is part of the Prosecution case that as involving the siege of East Mostar, that one of the things that the HVO did, and it's part of the Prosecution allegation in this case --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: -- is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me. We have a witness present and I understand that he may be testifying in relation to some events. I don't think it's proper for Mr. Scott -- I know he's not doing it intentionally --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The point is this -- I won't talk about anything specifically, but if there is something in the indictment and that's part of the case and, as we discussed some weeks ago, the Defence don't agree to anything, they dispute everything, that leaves the Prosecution no alternative but to put on proof of every point in the indictment that we think that is charged in the indictment. So I could take the Chamber to a number paragraphs in the indictment, but because the witness is present in the courtroom, I certainly won't do that. Final comment, Your Honour: In terms of the exhibits being listed in the pre-trial brief, I can assure the Chamber that at no time would every exhibit, would all 9.000 exhibits have ever been linked in the pre-trial brief. Probably they will not all be linked in the final trial brief. It's a selective process. The pre-trial brief is to orient the Chamber to the case. You might choose some exhibits but it would never under any scenario have listed every exhibit that the Prosecution contemplates possibly using in the case. Prosecution is doing everything we can to provide the Chamber with as much information and guidance as possible, Your Honour, and we will continue to do so. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you, Mr. Scott. Yes, sir, could you please rise. Sir, I greet you on behalf of my colleagues, Judges of this Chamber. Before you read out the solemn declaration, would you please tell me your name, your last name, your date of birth, and your occupation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... as you like it. My name is Edward Vulliamy, I was born on the 1st of August, 1954, in London, Great Britain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, and what is your occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you already testified in any cases before the International Tribunal? If so, then in which cases?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have, Your Honour. I've testified a number of times here in cases against -- I endeavour in chronological order: Dusko Tadic, Milan Kovacevic, what I think is General or Colonel-General Blaskic, what I think is known as the Keraterm case against a number of defendants briefly, and latterly, against Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Can you please read out the text of the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will be very brief in my introductory remarks because you are not the first time here before the International Tribunal. First you will be asked -- answering questions put to you by the Prosecution. Then following that you will be examined by the Defence counsel and perhaps even some of the accused if there is a need for that. They might also put some questions to you during cross-examination. I have to remind you that you just swore to tell the truth, which means that you have to tell the truth and not lie. So your testimony is scheduled to proceed in the following way: Your examination-in-chief will take place today and then cross-examination tomorrow. And now I turn the floor to Mr. Mundis who will be putting questions to you on behalf of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, can you briefly tell the Trial Chamber your professional background.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. I -- briefly. I became a journalist properly in the late 1970s on a programme called World In Action for Granada television, a documentary programme working in all parts of the world, specialising in the conflict in Northern Ireland in my case. I moved to the Guardian in 1986, and as of 1989, was working mainly overseas as what I suppose one could call an international reporter, starting off in Eastern Europe, proceeding to work, in theory, from Italy but also across Yugoslavia, former Yugoslavia, and then to the United States, then back in Yugoslavia, and now back in London -- sorry, back to the United States again and now back in London. Forgive me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Vulliamy, just for clarification purpose, the Guardian is a newspaper based in the United Kingdom; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: It's a daily paper based in London, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us what awards, if any, you have won for your reporting and writing.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: 1985, I think, the Royal Television Society award for something in Northern Ireland; 1992/3 I won International Reporter of the Year; and Amnesty International Reporter of the Year; a thing called Granada, What the Papers Say; Reporter of the Year for work on Bosnia. In 1994 I won something called the James Cameron Award, pompously called the "British Pulitzer," for work on Bosnia and on some aspects of Italian violence in Italy. 1997 I won the International Reporter of the Year for work on Bosnia, and latterly I was runner-up for a couple of awards for work on trafficking in young women and Iraq.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, in addition to your newspaper writing, have you done any other published writing?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I wrote a book about the first year or so of the war in Bosnia called "Seasons In Hell." I wrote another book about corruption in British politics, and I've done various bits of television and radio broadcasting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, you alluded to the time that you were in Northern Ireland. Can you tell us about any -- and the former Yugoslavia. Can you tell us about any reporting that you've done from conflict zones.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Well, Northern Ireland was my speciality as a student. I returned there professionally many times. That was urban warfare, terrorism, urban warfare. Then I went to Lebanon briefly in 1982, to Beirut. I covered the immediate lead-up to and aftermath of the 1991 war in Iraq. I was there for a long time after that. And before the conflict in Bosnia I had been in Slovenia and in Croatia during 1991, and I have been to Iraq twice during the current whatever it is, conflict, and I have also worked in sort of places that one would regard as unsafe if not at war, like Haiti, Central America, and other places of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me turn the focus of your attention now, sir, to Bosnia. Can you tell us the first time during the conflict in Bosnia that you went to that country.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. This would be the -- well, briefly in the spring of 1992, but my first serious work there was in August of 1992 in the Prijedor region and pertaining mostly -- although I was also in Sarajevo around that time, my work pertained mostly to the attempt to expose and get into camps run by the Bosnian Serbs for Muslim and Croat inmates, and we did manage to find a way in to those at Omarska and Trnopolje, and my work also involved, when I arrived in Bosnia, the whole question of enforced deportations from that region of mostly Muslims but a number of Croats into Central Bosnia at gunpoint. I walked with them, followed them on those enforced deportation convoys.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And again, Mr. Vulliamy, for purposes of clarification, at this period of time in the middle of 1992 or into the autumn of 1992, who was the perpetrator of the crimes that you were covering that you just mentioned to us?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: In the north-west, the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: In how long following these incidents that you've told us about in August of 1992 in Prijedor, after that how long did you remain in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Well, I was on a rota of reporters assigned to cover the war, so I was there on and off between that period and February, 1994, when, against my wishes, actually, I was transferred, or promoted, to Washington, and I returned at my own request - I demoted myself, I suppose - to go back in the summer of 1995, and I stayed there for the end of the war and then went back during 1996 to do a retrospective series. So on and off, summer 1991 -- in the former Yugoslavia, summer 1991 to spring 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let's go back, sir, to the period after late summer, 1992, when you told us about the camps in Prijedor. Can you give us a brief chronology of where your reporting duties in Bosnia took you after the autumn of 1992 or during the autumn of 1992.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. They took me immediately to Herzegovina. Do you want me to give an overview or to go --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Perhaps --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: -- if you could just give us an overview first and we'll go back and ask some follow-up questions.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I'm sorry. I was working across Herzegovina, up in Central Bosnia, in Mostar. That would cover the autumn, the summer into the fall, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let's -- let's focus now on Herzegovina. You told us at line 20, "they took me immediately to Herzegovina." Your travels that took you to Herzegovina, can you tell us approximately when you went there in the autumn of 1992?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Our exposure of the camps at Omarska and Trnopolje created quite a lot of impact, and a sort of media circus descended on those places. A challenge came from the Serbs that there were camps in which their people were being held on the other side, and I thought it fair enough to, you know, in the interests of, I suppose balance if not pushing the agenda, to investigate those, and Capljina was a name given. I had never heard of the place. So via Hungary and Zagreb, I would have left Belgrade about the 8th or 9th of August, and via Zagreb down to Capljina, would have arrived there sometime -- I wouldn't want to put an exact date on it, probably around the 10th to 11th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, you just told us that the challenge came from the Serbs that there were camps in which their people were being held on the other side. Can you tell us what you mean or what you interpreted that to mean when you were told that they were being held on "the other side"?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Well, I mean -- what Nikola Koljevic the then deputy head of the Bosnian Serbs meant, I think, was we had just uncovered horrific, horrific places in which Muslims and Croats were being held by the Bosnian Serbs. Their allegation was that we would find similar on the other side. By "the other side," he meant the alliance between the Bosnian army and the HVO, Bosnian Croatian -- Bosnian Croat militia, army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, if you could continue with what you experienced or witnessed when you went down into Capljina approximately the 10th or 11th of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Well, we arrived in Capljina -- we did actually go and see a leading politician before we went to Capljina, but in Capljina itself, we -- and this is me myself and a woman from the Associated Press, and of course a translator, but we went to Capljina to the headquarters of the organisation that we were told ran this particular camp, which was the HOS, a -- not the HVO. The -- the military wing of a party called the Croatian Party of Rights, and we went to their headquarters and met with their commander, in pursuit of permission to go to this camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did -- can you tell us who that person was?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: His name was Milan Dedakovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What, if anything, did Mr. Milan Dedakovic do for you?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Well, he was a swashbuckling fellow, not ashamed of his own -- I'm not sure "charisma" is quite the word, but he was a confident man, and we talked about a recent apparent execution of one of his -- one of his commanders, HOS commanders, in the area by the HVO, and we talked a lot about the politics of the rivalry between those two militias which pertained to his allegation that the HVO and the president of the Croatian Union of Herceg-Bosna, as it was called, Mate Boban, who we'd seen the previous evening, I think, he accused them of wanting to carve up Bosnia with the Serbs while he and his militia and its party insisted that all of Bosnia was Croatian and that that was the background for the internecine, well, argument, and indeed violent argument between them, and in his words, the execution of his commander. What we wanted from him -- and there was a lot of banter as well. What we wanted from him was permission to go into this camp and inspect it, and that he granted us, I have to say more easily and more readily than I'd expected.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, I'll ask you some follow-up questions about that in just a moment, but I'd like to return to something that you just told us, and that is as reflected on line 22 of the transcript, where you made reference to Mate Boban and you said "who we'd seen the previous evening." Do you recall any of the events that happened when you met with Mr. Mate Boban?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. I recall -- I recall the meeting well. It was at his office in a town called Grude, a small town and quite a menacing place although there was no actual fighting there. We knew who he was. Each community or people, if you like, in Bosnia had a leading figure, and Karadzic in the case -- Radovan Karadzic in the case of the Bosnian Serbs, the President Alija Izetbegovic in the case of the -- of the Bosnian Muslims, and Mate Boban was very much the name that one associated with the apex of power among the Bosnian Croats. He was not, and I'll say just this at this point unless you want to pursue, he was not actually the president of the main Croatian -- Bosnian Croat party, which was the HDZ and a Bosnian wing of the ruling party in Zagreb of President Franjo Tudjman, but he was the president of something called the Croatian Union of Herceg-Bosna or the Croatian - what did they call it? - Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. And he talked to us at that meeting about his plans for that entity and how he was going to achieve it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Before I ask you about the plans, sir, do you recall the approximate date that you had this meeting with Mr. Boban?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Well, it will have to be approximate, I'm afraid. It's -- travelled on the 12th. It's the -- it's -- it's just before the middle of August. If I can guess it, it's 12, 13, 14th of August, something of that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Of which year?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us now about what you recall from this meeting where plans for the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna were discussed with Mr. Boban.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, he made it clear -- and he was, incidentally, willing and wanting to have this conversation. He made it clear that he did not and could not recognise the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina nor could he recognise Sarajevo as its capital. The reason he gave was that the constitution guaranteed the rights of individuals but not of people, and the word he used for people was "narod" which is an important word because it means people as an ethnicity or it is -- it is -- it doesn't mean people going shopping, it means a people, the "Hrvatski Narod," the Croatian people. He then went on to describe in some detail how he wanted the various "narod" Serbian Muslims and Croatians to be divided within Bosnia by a system of what he called cantons or provinces, which he likened, I think for sort of public relations reasons, to Switzerland and the European Union, and how one group of these cantons or provinces would be specifically Croatian. He talked about how Herceg-Bosna was connected to Croatia, and the words he used were culturally, spiritually, and economically, and he said that it -- that Herceg-Bosna had been separated from Croatia by what he called "unfortunate historical circumstances." And he then talked about the HVO as specifically -- he -- he didn't -- he didn't talk about the HVO in relation to the HDZ, to his party, but he talked about them as the legitimate military force on what he called the free territory, and went on to make some remark that -- of a nature that the Croatian people were ready to arm to defend this freedom, as he put it, which was language which my experience told me was not always defensive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, did you ask Mr. Boban to elaborate upon the unfortunate historical circumstances that he referred to?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I think we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again, if I may intervene for a second, Mr. President, and I can understand the difficulties that Mr. Mundis may be having, but it is leading in nature. I can see and I can sense that Mr. Vulliamy is struggling to remember what he wrote in his -- in his statement. I don't object to him having his statement present. If he doesn't recall exactly, he may look at it to refresh his memory if that may assist, but I would object to any leading questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, page 28, line 6 and 7, the witness just testified that "Herceg-Bosna had been separated from Croatia by what he called unfortunate historical circumstances." Those are the words that came from the witness. I have simply asked him if he asked Mr. Boban to elaborate upon or explain what he meant by the use of that term. That's not something that I created; it came right from the mouth of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I will withdraw the objection. I stand corrected.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I -- sorry, after all that I don't actually remember the exact nature of the conversation. I think we did the -- I think initially I took it to mean something to do with the Second World War or the end of the Second World War. On reflection, I think it might have had something to do with the fact that Croatia had fought for and secured its independence from Yugoslavia in 1991, whereas Bosnia had come on behind and had secured its independence only in the spring of 1992. But I don't know if that's what he meant, but that was a discussion we had afterwards, trying to infer what he meant by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall any of the other issues or specific things that were discussed during this meeting, this initial meeting that you had with Mr. Boban in -- on or about the 13th, 14th of August, 1992?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Well, it was a long conversation, and the conversation about provinces and cantons went on -- you know, it was a long time. The other thing that was of interest was that there were -- there were reports, although they were in the back of one's mind, of a sort of a deal, a carve-up of Bosnia - and these are not reports that I had written; I had read them - between President Tudjman and President Milosevic of Serbia at a meeting they'd had somewhere in the Vojvodina area. I can't remember the name of the place, I think it began with K. And there had also been reports of a meeting between Mate Boban and Radovan Karadzic in Graz in Austria. We asked him if he'd ever met Radovan Karadzic, and he said no. I don't recall any particular details of that conversation in -- specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately how long this meeting with Mr. Boban lasted?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I would say between an hour and two.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What, sir, were your -- as a professional reporter, what impressions did you leave this meeting with?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Well, two: One, I was and we were, and we discussed this afterwards in the car, surprised at how the sort of -- that it had all been directed by implication and -- and overtly against the government in Sarajevo and against his allies on the Bosnian government side and indeed the Bosnian government army, by implication, because -- and it was all the stranger because only a matter of weeks beforehand, when I wasn't in the area, I think in late July, the alliance between the armija of BH, the Bosnian army, and the HVO had enjoyed perhaps its greatest moment by successfully pushing the Serbian positions, the Bosnian Serb positions back out of Mostar and uphill into the mountains, and they'd done that together, and that was a famous and much celebrated victory. And it seemed to me odd that Boban -- there didn't seem to be any -- I mean, he didn't seem to be revelling in that as I'd expected him to, nor did he seemed -- he didn't want to talk about it much. He seemed to want to be concerned with carving out this -- this Herceg-Bosna and its -- and its -- and establishing its relationship with Croatia. And I was surprised because his -- his remarks were sort of targeted much more at his own side, his ally, if you like, than at the people over whom he and his allies had just won a very major victory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, if you had any discussions with Mr. Boban at this point in time concerning the scope of Herceg-Bosna, the geographic scope of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I don't think -- I'm afraid I don't recall asking -- I mean, I knew Central Bosnia by then, but I don't recall asking him how far up into Central Bosnia he considered Herceg-Bosna to go, but I mean I took it to mean that the cantons did not just restrict the area he was talking about to Herzegovina itself, but I don't recall asking him for any map or border.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me return to something that you said a few moments ago. This is reflected on page 26, lines 13 and 14 of the transcript. You told us that this meeting was "at his office in a town called Grude, a small town and quite a menacing place." Again, that's lines 13 and 14 of page 26 of today's transcript. Can you elaborate, sir, upon what you meant by "a menacing place"?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Well, I mean, both in -- both in this war and in previous wars I'd got used to places where I didn't feel comfortable. I didn't feel threatened, but let's put it that although there was no fighting, there was the odd rasp of machine-gun fire into the sky. There were some very heavy lads around who weren't giving us very welcoming looks. The -- I didn't particularly like the fact that the portrait of Ante Pavelic, who was the Ustasha dictator in the Second World War, was in the windows of some of the shops, nor did I find it very tasteful that the U - a sort of capped U - of that movement had been painted on some of the walls. I didn't feel that I -- that I was at risk, but it was an uncomfortable place to be, and it was an intimidating place and a heavily militarised one although it was nowhere near any front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What do you mean by "heavily militarised"?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Well, there was -- there were -- there were a lot of soldiers, not -- not drilling or anything but sort of hanging around from both -- well, mostly from -- most of the number plates were HVO white number plates but there are a few HV number plates there as well, which are yellow.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And can you just tell us how you came to know that HV number plates were yellow.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Well, I'd spent a lot of time in Croatia, and even before there was such a thing as the HV, but all around the Dalmatian coast, I mean there is -- there are a lot of military -- there's still military movement going on. You -- you drive down from Zagreb or from Sibenik and you see -- you see HV as a yellow number plate. HVO was a white number plate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, what types of clothing these people that you told us were in the military were wearing?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: At this point, actually, various sorts of clothing. I mean, the HVO would have a uniform, but there were sort of lots of boys with, say, maybe a black T-shirt and a pair of camouflage trousers. I mean, some were in uniform, others were in semi-uniform. I didn't in Grude actually see any people in a HOS uniform, which is an all black uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I note the time. I'm about to move into a different subject. Perhaps this would be an appropriate time for the first break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll have a 20-minute break now, and we will resume in 20 minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing will now resume. Mr. Mundis, please take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, during the break I was asked, as I anticipated that I would be, to ask you to slow down a little bit in your answers for the sake of the court reporter. Let me --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, I will. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me turn your attention now to something that you spoke about earlier this afternoon and that is when you obtained permission from Mr. Dedakovic to visit a camp in Capljina. Can you tell us a little bit more about what happened.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Certainly. We left -- he didn't come with us. We left his -- his office, his headquarters, and arrived at a gate of a camp. I don't think word had been sent forward, or I didn't get the impression that it had been sent forward that we were to come because the commander of the camp, whose name was Hrstic, major, I think, was surprised and not that happy that we'd come in, but the order paper was clear. There may have been some telephone communication, I don't know. There was a Bosnian army sentry on the gate, which I could tell from the patch on his arm, but all the other guards were HOS, in the all-black HOS uniform. And we began after, I think, quite a long conversation with Hrstic, which I don't particularly recall details of, a sort of tour of the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And again, Mr. Vulliamy, for the record can you tell us the approximate date and time that you arrived at this camp.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: It will have to be approximate. We're talking mid-August; 14, 15, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, was it before or after the meeting that you had with Mr. Boban?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I think it was the day after.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the approximate time of day that you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: It would have been I imagine mid -- late morning through midday to early afternoon, that kind of time. No, maybe afternoon, because we did spend quite a long time with Dedakovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us approximately how long you remained in the camp on that day?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I should think in total two hours, most of which was talking to -- I mean a lot of which was talking to Hrstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did there ever come a time, sir, when you learned the name of this camp or location that you were at?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: At the time I didn't know the name. With hindsight, I do because I found myself back there at some other time on another -- on another occasion. I didn't know the name of the camp, no. It was listed on the list in Belgrade as Capljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, when you later, as you put it, found yourself back there, at that point in time, did you know the name of this camp?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. I returned there in September 1993, and the name of the camp was Dretelj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, can you describe for the Trial Chamber what you observed during the time period that you were in this camp in mid-August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. There were -- the prisoners were Serbs, and those that we were allowed to talk to in Major Hrstic's presence were all male Serbs of varying ages. There was -- there was a particular -- I mean, we'd just been in Omarska -- or I had just in Omarska and Trnopolje, and with that -- and with them in mind, I would say that the -- the -- what was saddening and distressing about this place was more to do with subjugation and extreme neglect rather than systematic killing or beating. The men were in bad condition, some in very bad condition, but not -- not through signs of beating or anything of that nature. There was a humiliating ritual of "rise," "sit," "thank you, Mr. Commandant," and there were some interviews with people of -- of -- I don't recall any greatly significant interview. What -- I mean in a way it was the high point -- the shock of the visit was as we were about to leave, we walked across a sort of yard or back towards the exit from where we'd conducted the interviews and past a shed on the right where a door was slightly ajar, a sort of sliding metal door. We could see clearly that the -- the -- that shed was full of large numbers of women, and we asked if we could go in there. We were told we couldn't. We were told in a fairly threatening way that we couldn't, elected not to insist, probably wrongly, and had a conversation about this with Major Hrstic afterwards during which I was threatened in a rather sort of bravado kind of way not to write or reveal the presence of these women in the camp. He made some joke about - what is it? - the less you know, the longer you live, or something, and he wasn't going to discuss it, but that was -- that was the thing that disturbed me most about that camp. And later on, back in Zagreb, we were talking about this to the Party of Rights, and there they were unable to enlighten me any further. But it was the presence of these women in the camp that alarmed me then and, with hindsight, alarms me even more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, at this point in time I'm going to ask you if you can take the narrative a little bit further in terms of what happened after you visited Dretelj. We will return, as you've told us, to the time in September, 1993, later in your testimony, but can you tell us where you went in -- towards the end of August or after you were in this Dretelj camp in August, 1993.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. I went back up to Travnik, and this was after quite a serious incident on Mt. Vlasic, which is a -- not part of perhaps what's relevant here. So that would have been towards the end of August. And on that visit I was very much sort of a guest of the HVO, because - excuse me - because my translator was a Croatian, a Bosnian Croat. She had friends in Travnik, and we stayed in -- I mean the system was -- it was called the Hotel Orient, and the system was that the hotels were militarised inasmuch as soldiers -- they were using the rooms and they were run by, in this case, the HVO, and the rooms were used by soldiers but, you know, for a few Deutschmarks they would let you stay while the soldier was out on night duty or something. So I got -- got to spend a lot of time on that visit talking to HVO people, and -- and a commander or deputy commander, I can't remember, called Pokrajcic, and we were sitting with him and somebody from the Bosnian army, a Muslim from the Bosnian army, and that was the first time I heard any discussion of problems between the two militias. And this man Pokrajcic, who was an estimable man, said I'm fighting for the victim peoples of this war, as he put it, and he actually even said over my dead body will I -- will I rupture the alliance, and he gave the impression, although I can't remember his exact words, that the pressure he was talking about was coming up from Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, the identity of the person that you've identified as a Muslim from the Bosnian army? Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt. Actually, I hate to interrupt but as we all saw we are here now discussing events in Travnik. Travnik is not one of the locations where any crimes happened charged in this indictment we are dealing with here. So actually I don't see the relevance, but if the Prosecutor is again charging us for something that is not specifically charged, then probably some more charges. I don't know really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Mundis, is this issue of any relevance, the issue of Travnik that you are discussing?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, the witness has spent a significant period of time in Bosnia. It's a chronological story that will allow us to go from one point to the next point. There are references in the indictment and in the maps and material that Your Honours have before you to events in Central Bosnia. Of course, Travnik is part of Central Bosnia. We would contend that this is also relevant to taking us in terms of a logical time line in progression through the events during the time period when this witness was in Bosnia. I'm not going to be dwelling on any significant -- for any significant period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour. The locations where crimes happened, and the crimes which are charged by the indictment are specifically defined in paragraphs 43 to 217 of the indictment, and it is not Travnik. It is definitely not Travnik. And by the way, the witness was talking about Omarska and some other places he visited in Bosnia-Herzegovina related to those about which he testified in other cases --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, that's not what Mr. Mundis said. Mr. Mundis said that we have a witness who was in that part of Bosnia during the period referred to in the indictment, and for the sake of historical context, it might be interesting to have a few guidelines. We're not talking about any crimes in this case, we are dealing with context. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, this period in August, 1992, how long did you remain in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: That visit, I should think three to four days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And where did you go after you left Travnik in August, 1992?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I think I went back home, which, by the way, was in Italy at the time, and returned a couple of weeks later. I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: When was the next time following this trip to Italy that you were in Bosnia, and what part of Bosnia were you in?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: It would have been September, and again I went up to Central Bosnia, Vitez, Travnik, around that time. I'm just trying to -- sorry, I'm just -- I'm finding the time line. Yes. I think I went up to Central Bosnia again in September.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And how long did you remain in Central Bosnia at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I don't recall, I'm afraid, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, when was the next time you were in Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I think the next time I was in Herzegovina was probably in October, towards the end of October, to the best of my recollection. Middle to end of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you describe for us the circumstances which took you back to Herzegovina in October, 1992.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. And that's -- that's a day I can remember, because I got to Split in the middle of October, and somewhere around 19th, 20th, the translator and/or my colleague from Reuters, who is a former Yugoslav himself, was reading in the paper that Mate Boban had been in Travnik, at the time which I already had relationships and quite good contacts in both the two allied armies, and he'd been there and pronounced it part of Herceg-Bosna. And that surprised me because Travnik is a majority -- although it had a strong HVO presence and a thriving Croatian community, it's predominantly a Muslim town. And I think we were still in Split, and I wish we'd hit the road immediately because we were still in Split when news came of a shoot-out at a gas station in Novi Travnik or Pucarevo, as it was called at the time, just to the south at a gas station and someone, a Muslim, had been killed. And it seemed that this was now a serious story and needed examining, and I hit the road I think on the 22nd to go to Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And when you heard this news, you were in Split?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Either in Split or on the way up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, the route that you travelled in October, 1992?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, I do, well, because it was through Kiseljak and up the Lasva Valley, through Busovaca, and then you turn left towards Vitez. And I remember it because there was a fair -- there was a substantial mobilisation going on, a movement of troops north, particularly from Kiseljak, and roadblocks, HVO roadblocks, coming up on -- onto that road both from Kiseljak up to the T-junction, and particularly towards Vitez. I'm talking about trucks and buses and there were other troops moving from the south, south of Kiseljak towards Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, where during this specific trip in October, 1992, where did you end up on that day? Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: We ended up in Vitez, hoping to stay the night. Again, hoping that the same system I described in Travnik at the Hotel Orient would pertain again; i.e., that even though the hotel had been taken over by the HVO, you could still get a room there if you paid them some money. Sorry, that sounds wrong; made a contribution. And the -- but at this time there was a marked difference. At the hotel, there were people there in -- bedding down in the bar area, in the reception area, to sleep. All the rooms were full. There was no deal to be done about staying there. This was now a militarised -- a completely militarised place. But we decided to stay around in Vitez. There was some small-arms fire going on, and I think through the HVO people at the hotel we ended up in a sort of makeshift radio studio listening to a debate in a small block of flats on the west side of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, at that point in time, and that is in October, 1992, were you aware of what party or parties were involved in this conflict whereby you heard small-arms fire?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Oh, yeah. Yes. I mean, as a follow-up of the news of the shoot-out in Novi Travnik. There was -- it was the HVO and the armija BH, or at least, if it wasn't the HVO and the armija BH, it was Muslims against Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, how long do you remain in Vitez in October, 1992?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Our plan to remain there -- we wanted to stay but we couldn't because after the radio broadcast I think we tried again at the hotel and again thought not, but the atmosphere was getting quite menacing because during this radio programme being recorded there was quite a lot of fighting around the edge of the Stari Vitez, Old Vitez area, which is the mainly Muslim bit. There was some fire coming out, and the fire going in accelerated during the radio debate because we could see it from the window. By then -- well, I easily knew the sound of an anti-aircraft weapon being fired ground to ground - it's a deeper sound - and that's what was being used.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And again, Mr. Vulliamy, how long did you remain in Vitez in mid-October, 1992?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Well, we left that night, unable to sleep, went to place called Fojnica, and then came back up at -- attempted to come back up to Vitez again the next day but we couldn't because we got stuck in some quite fierce fighting on the edge of Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, where did you then go after this incident where you were stuck on the edge of Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Well, we were stuck there for quite a long time with a group of HVO soldiers in an exchange of fire, and then we did finally get through Vitez to Travnik and went to the hospital in Travnik where the victims of this new embryonic, and I have to say rather shocking, confrontation were, many of them children.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And where did you go next, sir?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Back down to Split to file the story. I should explain: There were no telephones available to us at that point in Central Bosnia, and you had to drive back to Split or a border town - there's one called Imotski - to file stories. There was a story to file, not least the fighting that we'd seen in Vitez and indeed been part of and pinned by quite -- and very frightened by in Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And on this occasion when you travelled to Split to file your story, can you tell us what route you took.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: We went through Konjic that -- that night. Why, I don't know. I wasn't driving. I'd hooked up with someone from the Sunday Times who had a vehicle by then. Why we went through Konjic I don't know, because it was being shelled by the Serbs, but we got back to Split okay. I don't know why we went that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And again, when did you then leave Split and where did you go next?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Well, almost immediately, because either on the way back, on the radio or when we got to Split, or a mixture of both, we heard that there was reason to go to Mostar, that an ultimatum had been made whereby the -- well, there were actually -- there were -- there were confused reports. There was one report that the Bosnian army was -- that the HVO no longer recognise the authority of the Bosnian army. There was another report that, quotes, Muslim extremists would no longer be tolerated on the free territory, and then there was a specific ultimatum from Mostar. Now, whether or not it meant within Mostar or from Mostar for the whole territory, I didn't know, but there was an ultimatum from Mostar that the Bosnian army had to either disarm or come under HVO authority. So the next morning we set off for Mostar. That -- that's the 24th or maybe the 25th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Of which month and year, please?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: October.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yeah. I think it's the 24th, counting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And did you in fact go to Mostar on that day?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: We did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And can you tell the Trial Chamber what events you witnessed in Mostar on that day?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: It was quite dramatic and impactful. The HVO had indeed put out their ultimatum. They had taken over important buildings in the city. The PTT - that's the telephone building - the court -- courts, the town hall. They put a guard outside the BH army headquarters. I should explain that at that time, because the alliance had been such a close and effective one, the two headquarters of the two armies were, if not next door, they were close neighbours on the west side of the city. And we got there, were told this -- well, you could see a lot of HVO activity on the streets. Went first to see the Bosnian army commander, whose name was Pasalic, and asked him about this ultimatum, and he said something to the effect of how can I disarm? I'm supposed to be fighting a war. That's not a direct quote. And something to the effect - again not a direct quote - that this is plan, that this is coming from the top. This is coming -- I think he did mention Grude specifically. And warned, and this is very early on, with hindsight, that if this plan was seen through to its professed conclusion, it would mean, and he said "war in Mostar." He told us that the HVO had come in and taken his radio system, and it was actually one of his aides who was a Croat from Zagreb, a student fighting in the Bosnian army, who showed us that -- the wires pulled out and everything from their radio communications room. He was very angry, this young Croat, at what had happened. And I think we then had a long conversation with -- with -- I think it must be the deputy commander. His name is Tetak. He was angry, afraid at what was going on. And said, We want to fight with these people together. Tetak said something to that effect: We want to fight for a united country.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you have any other meetings while you were in Mostar during this period of time on or about the 24th of October, 1992?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, several meetings that day, the next of which was next door with the commander of the HVO. If he wasn't the commander, that's -- he was the deputy or at least a senior figure. His name was Lasic. I don't know his first -- I mean, I did and somewhere written, probably, his first name, but I can't recall it. And his headquarters was buzzing with troops, weapons. He produced a rather good -- good scotch whisky, and made his -- yes. He outlined what -- to us what was going on in his terms. He called the HVO the civilian military authority in Mostar and gave the impression that so far as representation was concerned in the civilian military, coupling the words together, authorities in the town, no, as he put it, Muslim, I don't think he actually mentioned the army in that point, would be represented. He said that the armija BH should be disarmed and said that he -- I think he -- he didn't say he demanded. He said, you know, I'm inviting them, or something, to come off the front line, the front line being to the east of the city at that point. We talked a lot about that remark afterwards because it has extreme military significance. That's all I can remember from that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, at that point in time do you know what front line was being referred to?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I presumed, and I think rightly, it meant the front line held by the Bosnian army and the HVO to the east of Mostar against the Serbs, but information talking to the Bosnian soldier -- soldiers later in the day informed us, rightly or wrongly, I have to say this is what we were told, was that the BH lines were further forward than the HVO lines, and by taking them off the front line, the HVO were actually retreating by some -- by some small distance. I mean, retreating the common front line, which militarily doesn't make sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, at this point in time - again 24 October, 1992 - what the conditions in Mostar were like for the residents of the city?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: The city had been under Serbian shell-fire ever since they were pushed out in July. We didn't talk much to residents that day but we did talk to refugees. Refugees, Muslim and Croat, from Serbian-held territory to the east and south-east, most of them. And the interesting thing about that, those conversations, was that they were all going to have to re-register with the HVO if they wanted to stay, that their papers, whatever those papers were, were no longer valid, and -- I think they must have been Bosnian government papers of some kind, were no longer valid, and they were all going to have to individually re-register with the HVO and get a newly stamped document to retain their status. I recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, did you notice anything that had changed from the last time you had been in Mostar in 1992?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Well, a lot more troops on the streets for sure. And let's see. I mean -- well, and -- and the cost of the Serbian shelling which had continued. There were, I think, even when I was there in -- in August there were graveyards in the parks and that sort of thing. I mean, the marks of war. But I did, on my previous visit, go over to the east side just basically because I wanted to see the bridge, and there was marginally more destruction from the shelling but not -- not markedly. What you noticed is the HVO had taken over and that everything that they had been talking about in Vitez was happening in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you have any other meetings on that day in October, 1992?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, one with a Muslim political figure whose name I can't remember, I'm afraid. He might have been in the SDA. The -- the -- the main Muslim party led by President Izetbegovic. I don't remember much about the conversation, but I remember him being very distressed and worried for the city and for -- and for the next few months. You know, I ought to say that it was still quite a shock despite all the warnings and despite what one perhaps should -- one should have made more of what Mate Boban had said back in August and heeded it as more of a threat to bring this about, but it was still quite a shock after, you know, one's work in the north-west, given what the Bosnian Serbs were meting out to both Serbs and Croats together, and given one's experience of the way in which they were allied elsewhere in the country, it was still quite a shock that this had happened so quickly, so efficiently, and so determinedly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, how long did you remain in Mostar during this visit on or about the 24th of August?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: No, we left that day, because we went to see Mate Boban. Left at dusk, went straight to Grude.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And can you tell us about this meeting that you had with Mr. Boban in Grude on the 24th of October, 1992.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. He'd moved across the road. He was now in a hotel, Hotel Grude. And we were sent down into the cellar, into the basement, to wait for him. He was having a meeting behind a curtain. It was some sort of dining or -- area that I think they'd turned into his headquarters in this hotel. We were told to wait. It was indicated that he would see us. We waited. This meeting broke up. The meeting was all with uniformed people. He was in a very good mood and welcomed us in and he was in a good mood because he said, I've just been made president of the HDZ. And we congratulated him and he congratulated us on the exclusive first interview with the party's new president in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, when you say, as you just did, that the meeting was all with uniformed people, can you tell us what kind of uniforms --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: -- these people wore? What can you tell us about your knowledge at this point in time, that is October, 1992, about the HDZ party?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Well, as I said before, to repeat briefly, the HDZ was the ruling party in Croatia, led by the president, Dr. Franjo Tudjman. It had a wing in Bosnia, which was -- in theory it was semi-autonomous but it was very close to Zagreb. But the quirk was that its leader was a man who I had not at that point met but later met and talked a lot with but of whose existence I knew, called Stjepan Kljuic. Kljuic was the leader of the party I think by necessity because he lived in Sarajevo.
