And although a very loyal Croat, he was also loyal to the alliance and to the Bosnian government, which he recognised. He thought that the HDZ was the best way to represent Croatian interests within a unified Bosnia, and certainly within the alliance. He -- I don't want to go into -- I don't want to jump the gun chronologically, but he later said that what happened to him that day we met Mate Boban was a putsch, and Mate Boban told us he was now the president. This, in one's mind, was perfectly coherent with all that we had seen and heard over the last couple of days, and so we were very anxious to talk to him and also talk to him about what was going on in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, do you recall any of the specific subjects that were discussed with Mr. Boban in Grude on 24 October, 1992?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, I do. We returned to this matter of cantons and provinces because I now wanted to know more about them. Again, I'm sorry to jump around chronologically, but we're a couple of months, I can't remember exactly how many, away from the Vance-Owen Plan, the peace plan drawn up by Lord David Owen and Cyrus Vance. And it, with hindsight, is extraordinary to look back on that conversation now because what Mate Boban said to us that night in developing his idea of a Herceg-Bosna made up of cantons almost exactly prologued the Vance-Owen Plan. In fact, when the Vance-Owen came around there was a joke it stood for "Hvala Vance-Owen," which means, "Thank you Vance-0wen." So he elaborated on that. He said that HVO was now the only effective army on the free territory, which-- well, might have been true of some parts of it if the free territory is to mean all that not controlled by the Serbs but is not true of other parts of it. But what also was going on at the time was the Geneva peace talks were either in progress or about to happen, I can't remember which, and he made it perfectly clear that he was now going to call the shots on behalf of the Bosnian Croats at Geneva, he used fairly threatening language with regard to anyone who would disagree with him, and I think he -- he said the HVO is now ready to assume supreme military authority in this area. He talked about that when we talked about Mostar and he used similar language when we did asked him specifically about Mostar. He was talking about Mostar and the territory of Herceg-Bosna. He called the army a purely Muslim militia. I remember that. Which actually was not true at that time. It was almost true later on in the war but at that time it was not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, let me interrupt you there and put to you a couple of follow-on questions. First, you just told us, page 50, line 6, that Mr. Boban made it perfectly clear that he was now going to call the shots. What -- what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Well, I mean I -- yes, I remember what he said. He said what he meant by that. He said something to the effect of no one is going to represent the Bosnian -- the Bosnian Croats at Geneva unless authorised by me or -- or following my policy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You also told us that --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yeah. Sorry. And his policy, as we understood it, that -- that -- at that meeting was -- and I think he singled out Karadzic as well. I mean, he said no dealing with Karadzic but he also said no dealing with Izetbegovic, no dealing with the Presidency in Sarajevo. I mean, it was -- it was a declaration of independence and implicitly of war at the same time. You must, Your Honours, remember that we'd had a lot of these conversations, if you will, from the Serbs in Croatia in 1991, from the Bosnian Serbs in early summer 1992. They invariably led to violence. They were invariably the prologue to violence, this kind of language.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you, sir: You told us -- again this is lines 8, 9 and 10 of page 50, you -- Mr. Boban said "the HVO is now ready to have supreme military authority in this area. He talked about that when he talked about Mostar." Do you recall in any more specifics the discussion on 24 October, 1992, with Mr. Boban concerning Mostar?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: He did make some reference that there will be no Muslims in the authority, that the Muslims will not be part of running this city any more. He had always insisted that Mostar was the capital of Herceg-Bosna and gave non-military reasons for that. We have to have a big city, I remember him saying, it's got a university; this kind of argument. On that occasion he did say in some way, and I cannot, I'm afraid, remember the exact words, that the Muslims will not be -- will not be taking part in the running of Mostar militarily or politically. And it is -- it is the capital of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Approximately how long did this meeting on this day with Mr. Boban last?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Again, I don't recall. I would say again between an hour and two.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And as you left the meeting that evening, do you recall what impression stuck in your mind from this discussion that you'd had with Mr. Boban?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. My colleague from Reuters and I discussed it on the way back to wherever we were staying that night. I can't remember, I think we did go all the way back to Split, actually. We -- we discussed the speed at which all this had happened, the efficiency with all -- with all this -- with which all this had happened, the -- now getting quite worried about what Boban and the HVO meant by such terms as used before, "to defend our freedom," "to become the supreme authority." As I said, you know, I'd had experience, well, in other places too but specifically in former Yugoslavia I'd had experience talking to the Serbs about Eastern Croatia and about -- with the Serbs about the Muslims in north-west Bosnia, and that kind of language tended to be, as I said, prefaced -- tended to preface violence, and there was no reason not to suppose it wouldn't do so again, because this was bellicose talk, and it was -- and it was sad, in a way, because it seemed that the alliance was now ruptured and deliberately so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, on lines 9 and 10 of page 52, you're quoted as saying, "We discussed the speed at which all this had happened, the efficiency with all -- with all this -- with which all this had happened." When you make reference to what had happened, what exactly are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Well, I'm referring, I think, to the -- to the HVO and -- and Boban stamping their authority on a territory they -- they were calling Herceg-Bosna, which apparently extended all the way up as far as Travnik and included Travnik, and -- and the -- the overt attempt to subjugate both -- well, they talked about Muslims, but certainly their allies within that territory and to effectively declare at least a degree of independence from -- from the country as -- as was with Sarajevo as a capital, which we had thought they were fighting to -- to -- to maintain, at least. Not any more we didn't, but that was the idea originally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, can you tell the Trial Chamber where you went in the days immediately after this meeting with Mr. Boban on the 24th of October, 1992.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: On the days immediately after, there was a -- there was an outing with the British army from Split when they were trying to work out routes into Sarajevo, aid routes, and they were trying one which went up through Mostar and a place called Tarcin, as I recall, and they were turned back by the HVO, which was surprising, because one might have expected to get turned back by the Serbs further up the line, as often happened, but not by the HVO. I went up into Central Bosnia and on to Vitez and Travnik to do something else connected with the -- with the -- with an attempt to get to Jajce, I think it was, and to cover the attempt to hold Jajce, which was a town north of Travnik held by the Bosnian army and the HVO against a Serbian siege, and then drove down towards Tomislavgrad and Split, I think to file a story on that, and went through the town of Prozor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Vulliamy, let me ask you, as you were going north from Mostar up to the Central Bosnia area, what route did you take on that occasion, travelling northbound?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I think we went back -- the British convoy turned round, went back, but I don't recall which route we took up into Central Bosnia, I'm afraid. But when we came back down, back down south, it was through Prozor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately what the date was when you went back down south through Prozor?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: It would have been a weekend. I'm afraid I can't give you the date. I would have written it somewhere. It can be worked out from published articles. It was either a Friday evening or a Saturday. A lot of people -- possibly even a Sunday, but I think a Friday evening or a Saturday. A lot of people out on the streets.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And can you describe the mood of the people you saw out on the streets on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: It was complete -- life was completely normal. In fact, shortly after going through the town we stopped for coffee. People on the streets, a weekend either beginning or about to begin, kids chatting. Prozor was a fair distance from any front lines. It was -- it was -- it was unshelled unless some Serbs had got some shells a very long way, and life was perfectly normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, after that occasion, did you ever return to the town of Prozor?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Indeed. We headed back up into -- filed whatever we were filing on -- from Central Bosnia, went back up, heading for -- to -- I can't remember where we were going. And this would be two, possibly three days later. And a group of us, and were astonished by what we found as we approached let alone arrived in Prozor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, can you please tell us the approximate date - day, month, and year - when you returned to Prozor on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I'm afraid -- I don't want to give you an exact date. We're talking end October.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And the year?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And approximately what time did you arrive in Prozor on this day towards the end --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Late afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us what you saw on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. The first thing we saw before we got to the town were a lot of soldiers, and between Prozor and -- between there is a village called Rumboci, and between there and Prozor, and especially on the high ground as you come into Prozor were a lot of artillery and, in English, a lot of graffiti, new graffiti, which read "Cro territory." Going down into the town, saying nothing other than Oh, my God, and things that shouldn't be repeated in a courtroom, let me say that the main street had been gutted, or most had been gutted. Rows of buildings, in some places every other building, in some places every fifth building, had been incinerated and were empty. There were signs of shelling, there were signs of small-arms fire. There were soldiers going through the shops, looting. In the area which I had took, rightly or wrongly, to be the Croatian area, which was fairly untouched, life was seemed to be -- I mean, the children were sort of hanging around on the streets, we stopped and talked only very briefly to one group of soldiers. I can't remember what they said. We were not anxious to hang around. The atmosphere was very frightening indeed, and we proceeded out of town, what I presumed to be the Muslim quarter of town, or at least the concentration of Muslims because they're mostly mixed in, is to the left as you leave the town and climb a hill. A lot of the houses in that area were damaged. There was some incineration although less than on the high street. The minaret was damaged although not blown down, as one had seen so often. I recall a dead horse lying in the road, for what that's worth. Otherwise, very little sign of any life of at all once you left the town until you got to the top of the hill, and there was a sort of mountain chalet or installation of some kind teeming with soldiers, heavy weaponry rivetting in, and the beginning a series of new roadblocks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, when you tell us that you saw soldiers in Prozor on this day, what type of clothing were these soldiers wearing?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: They were almost all in fatigues of one kind or another, and I noted - and I'm still not quite clear why - that a lot of them had red ribbons on their epaulettes, but they were mostly in military -- military uniform or -- I have actually since seen a picture of somebody in -- which I didn't see on the ground, in a sort of neo-Nazi uniform, but that doesn't really count for much. They were mostly in military uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you, Mr. Vulliamy, at any point subsequent to this file any type of stories concerning events in Prozor on this day?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, that night. This was -- this was a shocking new development. I think it's fair to say that we knew by now that this alliance had ruptured because we'd seen what we'd seen in Vitez, and we'd seen what we'd seen in Mostar, and the roadblocks, plus the mobilisations, et cetera. But this was, and I dislike the word but it's in the vocabulary, this was ethnic cleansing. This bore all the hallmarks of that which I'd seen so much of by the Serbs in Eastern Croatia, by the Bosnian Serbs in the north-west of the country. I say all the hallmarks; it didn't look like some of those areas, or as bad as some of those areas I've just mentioned, but it was the same -- it -- it -- it had the same flavour to it. It didn't feel that there had been a battle between militias in Prozor, it felt as though the Muslims had been burned out. We got as far as Travnik that night with some difficulty because there was some fighting, or at least there was some distant shooting in Novi Travnik, and it turned out that the headquarters of the Bosnian army had all that time had a land-line and in this extremity allowed us to use it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, were you ever at any point in time involved in making a film production about the events in Prozor in 1992?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: No, I made a film later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: When did you make that film?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I first went to make -- went to Bosnia to make it in January 1993, and stayed there I think it was into February.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And what was the -- what was the basis for producing this film? How did you actually go about making the film?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: It was -- it was actually for a -- a religious affairs programme for the BBC, and the idea was -- it was called "Bosnia's Last Testament," and it was a sort of lament for what I saw at the time as being the end of a way of life in the town of Travnik, the end of a -- well, in a -- sorry, it was two things: It was the potential end of a way of life in Travnik. I mean, we can talk about this a bit more if it's permissible, but you know I felt that this was a country in which people had for so long learned to live together and wanted -- and so many of them still wanted to live together so the film was a sort of an aspiration that that may still happen and a lament for the fact it seemed to be falling apart.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, what was your role in the production of this film?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I was to write and present it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, with the assistance of the registry, I'd ask that the video marked as P1784 be shown to the witness by way of Sanction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: "... state within Bosnia calling itself Herceg-Bosna." "To the south of Travnik one night in October I stopped for coffee in the busy main street. A few days later I returned to find Croatian MUPs roaming through town and 5.000 Muslims driven into the mountains, looking for caves in which to hide. The pillage and killing in Prozor was the start of a new Bosnian war and a bitter betrayal for the Muslims. This is the consolidation of a hard-line Croatian mini state within Bosnia calling itself Herceg-Bosna. This territory flies a Croatian flag, has a Croatian puppet government, uses Croatian money, and even has special Croatian number plates, and it must say its rulers, come under a Croatian army. Bosnian who refuse that authority are dealt with in the time honoured way."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, the clip that we just have just seen, can you tell us what your role in producing that clip was.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: No. That's a library clip. I recognise it from the film but it was put in by the producer of the programme. I wasn't involved in the editing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And we noticed, sir, on the top of that clip a date in April, 1993. Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I can't, I'm afraid. I have no idea. It could -- it could be the date of the transmission, it could be the date that the BBC recorded it, I don't know. But if that's Prozor, which it looks like, that's not the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Vulliamy, on this day that you've been telling us about, how long did you remain in Prozor on that day?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Oh, very little time indeed. I mean, apart from a very cursory conversation with some of the soldiers, we drove straight out. It was frightening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, I neglected to ask you in terms of that video clip, at the end when you make reference to "the time honoured way," what were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I was referring to that which I'd mentioned earlier on, the time honoured way in which Croats had been expelled from eastern parts of their country in 1991, in which Muslims had been expelled from the Prijedor area in 1992. It was an attempt at a dry -- a dry reference to the -- yes, the time honoured way. It was by then a time honoured way. What I meant was you get them out, you burn them out, you bus them out; get them out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, can you tell us how that scene we just saw on the videotape compared with the events that you personally witnessed in Prozor at the end of October 1992?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: The streets look the same. The -- the lads look a bit sort of more like ruffians than the ones we saw, and I noticed that they didn't have these red ribbons on their soldiers, which for -- which stayed in my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: On this day after you left Prozor, can you please tell us where you went.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: We went to Travnik -- oh, we went to Travnik to file the story.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And how long did you remain on that occasion in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Oh, one night and left early in the morning to answer the question where -- where are -- where are the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, how did that question come to be formulated in your -- in your mind?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: The commander of the Bosnian army who -- who offered us the phone line -- I shouldn't. Anyway, he said, "All I know is that he -- is that the --" we were telling him as much as he could tell us. And what he said to us is that 500 -- all I know is that 5000 Muslims are missing from Prozor and we don't know where they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Where did you go the following day?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: We got up and went down back towards Prozor, but before we got to Prozor, on a junction we saw some women straggling - it was raining - up a road turning off to the left, and stopped to talk to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the approximate time that you arrived at this junction near Prozor?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I suppose it would have been late morning coming up midday-ish. I mean, it's not -- it's not an easy drive. Some -- something around that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And can you please describe for us what happened when you encountered these people that you -- or these women straggling, as you told us and stopped to talk to them. Would you describe for us what happened.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. We asked them what had happened. One of them, I noticed, was wearing bedroom slippers. They looked frightened, they looked bedraggled, and one of them said that they'd spent the night looking for caves, that soldiers were out killing people and looking for them. And as we were having this conversation, a mini cab pulled up. That sounds strange. He wasn't touting for business. He was a driver whose car happened to -- you know, he was a mini cab driver using his car in this emergency. And he told the women to get into his car, and those that wouldn't fit got into ours, and he told us to follow him, which we did, a little way up this road, and then turning off to the right up a track mountain track, and the track rose up through I think some wooded country and then opened out onto open -- open country, and there was this amazing sight of large numbers of people wandering the fields in groups or standing, looking to get away. Looking for somewhere. I don't know what they were looking for. They were wandering the open country.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, can you give us a rough approximation as to how many people you saw wandering the country on that day?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: It's difficult. I don't -- I hate numbers. Hundreds. Scores if not hundreds.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And which direction were these people wandering?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: In the direction of Jablanica, which I knew to be a government army-held town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And approximately how far from the town of Prozor were you at the point in time when you saw these people?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I'm not really sure. It's -- it's not far. Five to 10 kilometres max.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you, sir, at that occasion have the opportunity to speak to any of those people?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, we did. We spoke to quite a lot of them to try and get a picture of what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall any of the information that any of these people conveyed to you?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. I will have written somewhere but cannot recall direct quotes, and I can remember some details. In essence, it seemed that -- that shelling had -- well, one man did say that his Croatian neighbours suddenly left the neighbourhood the day before this happened. It seems that shelling began during the night or towards dawn. At dawn, soldiers moved into the town. It's -- it's a pattern I by this time knew well. It's the latter bit called -- it's called flushing out. Interviewees, I can't remember their names, I'm afraid. One woman told me that she had spent the night hiding in the cellar before escaping along a gutter or some kind of sewage trench. And one of the militarymen, men in military uniform up there, because there were a few ushering them about, said that he had seen bodies towed away on a trailer by a tractor, and others talked about having seen columns of men being marched out of the town. This is what -- what they were saying. The conclusion was that -- or my inference was that the town had been shelled first, that the soldiers had then gone in, and that these people had fled.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, you mentioned men in military uniforms ushering the people about. Approximately how many uniformed men did you see in this area?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: A few, not that many.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What type of --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: But they were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What type of arms did they have, if any?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I don't even know if they had any weapons. They might have done. I can't remember. I mean, they might have. I don't recall any rifles. They might have had revolvers. I don't recall any machine-guns or Kalashnikovs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, how long did you remain in this area where these people were straggling, as you put it?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Couple of hours or so. Oh, three -- three or four hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you describe the weather conditions at the time?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: At first wet and becoming drizzly. I mean difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What type of belongings, if any, did these people have with them?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Hardly anything at all, although I think a few may have had some plastic -- plastic bags full of things. I don't recall that they had much with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And how were these people dressed?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Oh, in -- in -- I mean -- I mentioned the bedroom slippers. They were people who had left in a hurry. They hadn't packed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, at any point in time did you have any discussions with any soldiers concerning Prozor and its significance?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, especially afterwards, given what had happened. And these were mostly soldiers from the United Nations, British soldiers from the so-called UNPROFOR. And -- well, actually, soldiers from both of the armies as well, but mostly British soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us what these discussions with UNPROFOR soldiers revealed to you?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. And this is later, and it made absolute sense, and although not a soldier myself, we had, as reporters, understood similar ourselves. Prozor -- the word "Prozor" means window, and the town of Prozor is the window, or perhaps better put, the gateway from Herzegovina into Central Bosnia up a road which, because of the situation regarding the conflict with the Serbs initially, was the lifeline -- one of the two lifelines for the delivery of aid into Central Bosnia, and for periods of time, because of risks to another route into Sarajevo, also the lifeline of aid into Sarajevo through Kiseljak and a Serbian checkpoint called Ilidza. So that was the significance of Prozor in terms of aid. Control Prozor, and you control, as it were, the portal of the aid route into Central Bosnia. When the UNPROFOR arrived, they tried to enhance some pieces of mountain track into proper and usable road in order to facilitate this -- this route, skirting properly metalled roads that were exposed to Serbian guns, and they called it Route Diamond. So we can think of Prozor as a kind of pivot on Route Diamond into Central Bosnia. And the other point, as I think we all knew anyway but which the British soldiers were quick to grasp, is that one man's aid route is another man's military supply route, and that Route Diamond was, of course, the HVO's, or one of the HVO's two - the other one through Kiseljak - two main military supply routes up into Central Bosnia. And it also meant that by controlling them, the Bosnian army in Central Bosnia was landlocked and had no access to the -- the -- because they used these same supply routes during the alliance, not just for whatever weaponry they could get but for gasoline supplies and so on. So it made absolute sense. If you wanted to start a putsch, a military putsch in Central Bosnia, you begin with Prozor. Civilian-wise, if I'm not wrong, it was one of the southernmost Muslim populations in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, line 19 of page 64 you told us the word "Prozor" means window. I would ask you if you know what language the word "Prozor" means window.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I have to confess I've never looked it up; I was told that. Serbo-Croat, or B/C/S as it's called now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me then ask you, sir, again, what steps, if any, you took to file a story following what you'd observed in this valley or this area near Prozor.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: We headed for the nearest telephone, which was in Tomislavgrad. Not a public phone, actually. There was a European Union Monitoring Mission man we knew there who -- and we thought we'd ask if we could use his phone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you describe for us who you had meetings with or discussions with in Tomislavgrad on that day, on that evening?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, briefly with this aforementioned Monitoring Mission man, but the -- the atmosphere in Tomislavgrad was one of jubilation, rasping machine-guns into the air. We'd actually followed a lot of the soldiers back in their trucks along the -- there's a track that runs from Prozor to Tomislavgrad, which may appear on maps as Duvno sometimes. They changed the name. The EU man was very insistent that we meet with a man who was introduced as the HVO commander in Tomislavgrad. Whether he was or not I don't know but he was introduced as such and invited to join us for dinner and we had a long -- tediously long conversation with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you there, Mr. Vulliamy. Do you recall the name of this person to whom you were introduced as the HVO commander in Tomislavgrad?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Shiljeg or Siljeg, and I can't remember his first name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall any of the details of this tediously long conversation that you had with him?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I can recall a few details. Well, I can recall one important detail: He said that Prozor was now clean. He made a reference to the -- the rather drunken celebrations outside as night games, as boys will sort of way. And then he got out a -- he got out a series of maps of Croatia down the centuries, 1 to 12, as I recall. Arduously went through each map as Croatia expanded and shrunk, and the last one I remember was labelled "Future Croatian Federation," and had Croatia extending all the way to almost to Belgrade, to a place called Zume. And it was the 1941 so-called Banovina Croatia. That was not actually HVO policy at all. It was, if anything, that of its old rival HOS. But it was a long, long lecture about history, as one had got quite used to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately how long this lecture lasted?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I don't recall how long, but way beyond exhaustion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And how long did you remain in Tomislavgrad?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I think we left the next morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall again the approximate date that this would be?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: No, but I remember why. Because I think I mentioned the siege of Jajce up in Central Bosnia. Word reached us if not that -- I think word reached us that night that Jajce was about to go, and by the time we woke up we heard that it had fallen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And again, sir, I understand you might not recall the date, but do you recall the month and/or year when you were in Tomislavgrad and learned that Jajce had fallen?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Unbelievably, I think we're still at the end of October. I think all this is happening at the end of October in rapid succession.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Vulliamy, upon hearing that Jajce had fallen, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Headed for Jajce. Jajce, not Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you in fact make it to Jajce on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: No. We tried to get into Jajce on previous occasions along a narrow corridor that linked Jajce to Travnik. The HVO and the Bosnian army used it to try and service the defence of the town from a heavy Serbian siege, Bosnian Serb siege. We tried to get up it a couple of times, it was terrifyingly dangerous, and abandoned our attempts on various occasions. And so we only got as far as a place called Turbe that night, which is a little bit far up the line from Travnik towards Jajce.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And did you spend the night in Turbe?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: No, we didn't. We went back to Travnik. There was some people coming in already, and we figured we'd get some sleep and get to work on this story the following day. We did talk to some of them and did interview a few people coming in, and they all told the same distressing story, that the siege had become unbearable, they'd been living in cellars, they hadn't been able to eat. But we went to sleep before we started doing our serious interviewing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And the following day when you awoke, can you tell us what you discovered.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I say this against myself: We discovered that we'd been wrong to go to sleep, because overnight the entire population of Jajce had arrived in Travnik, and it was an extraordinary sight of people sitting all over every bit of street with their broilers, their animals, their families, maybe a few possessions. So we quickly started up the road towards -- that was coming into town against the tide of this procession, this wretched procession, and started doing interviews with the -- with the people. Among them, by the way, were wounded soldiers, non-wounded straggling soldiers, what was left of each of these two armies, and they were coming by cart, on foot, horse-drawn cart if they had them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, when you say you started doing interviews with the people, did that include these soldiers?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: No. We didn't talk to any military people until later in the day, towards the evening time. We were trying to get a -- as vivid a sense as we could of the conditions under which Jajce had fallen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, Mr. Vulliamy, what you learned from any of the soldiers that you spoke to later on that day.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Well, there was an oddity and a curiosity. The soldiers were told -- I didn't see this happen, but I understood that their orders were to report to the respective headquarters of their armies in Travnik, and there were -- when we went and -- we went to see this, didn't -- didn't talk to many people, but when we got to the Bosnian army headquarters, there were some Croatians there, Bosnian Croats there, and along with some of the other soldiers they were wearing a patch that I hadn't seen before which had the Bosnian lilies in the top left corner and the Grb, the Croatian red and white chequerboard icon symbol in the lower right-hand half. You know, very obviously a symbol of the alliance. These were young soldiers, except one of them's father was there, and they wanted to register with the Bosnian army. They were talking about a sellout, they were talking about a deal, they said that we could have defended the town, and one of them said -- in fact, one actually mentioned Boban by name, said we're not going to fight Mate Boban's war against the Muslims. I should add that conversations with -- with the Bosnian army commander and one of the senior HVO officers in town that night did not bear out what they said. They said simply that Jajce -- that the defence had become untenable.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall, Mr. Vulliamy, the identity of either the Bosnian army commander or the senior HVO officers in town that you spoke to on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: The Bosnian army commander was -- was a man who I'd met a few times called Haso Ribo, and the HVO man's name I don't recall. I don't think he was the commander. I think -- no. It wasn't Pokrajcic, it wasn't the man I'd met before, nor was it, I don't think, the commander whom I would come to know later when I went back to Travnik in January.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. But just so we're clear, sir, at this occasion how long did you remain in Travnik at the end of October, 1992?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I think we -- I don't recall, but I think we must have left to file the story on the fall of Jajce. I can't -- that needed getting to London. I can't see that we'd have stayed around more than another night.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And to file the story in London, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: You had to go down to, if not Split, you had to go to one of the Croatian border towns where the phones worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, noting the time, I would suggest this is perhaps the appropriate point for the next recess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's about 5.20. We'll have a 20-minute break and resume in 20 minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, you have another hour and 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, right before the break we were talking about the events at the end of October, 1992, and you went to file your story on the fall of Jajce. Can you tell us how long you remained in Bosnia after you filed that story at the end of October, 1992?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I think I left pretty soon afterwards. One of my friends, a Croatian cameraman for the BBC, was killed that night. We had to arrange for his body to come back. I was disinclined to stay around. I didn't come back until January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And can you tell us, Mr. Vulliamy, when you first came back in January, 1993, where you entered Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: In through Split, as usual. This is with the BBC now, to make this film. And we went up -- ah, yes. Well, we had to go through Kiseljak this time because we were told that Route Diamond was effectively shut, and we didn't have guaranteed use of an armoured vehicle. At some point around this time, I think a little later in the year, the -- the British wouldn't actually let you go up Route Diamond unless you had an armoured vehicle, which I didn't, I was just driving a red Citroen, so it was necessary to go through Kiseljak. Then up the Lasva Valley towards what I'll call the Vitez T-junction, and that was a memorable drive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And at this point in time, that is January, 1993, how long did you remain in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I think a couple of weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And where did you go next, sir?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: It was all -- the film was about Travnik. It was centred around Travnik. But for some reason, and it must have been accommodation, the -- the stay involved a lot of driving, sometimes by night, between Travnik and Kiseljak, and that's -- that's why -- the scene along that road had been transformed and my car took a bullet. There was a lot of shooting. Few cars. Those that were on that road, a lot were being shot at and shot off it. So I was between Travnik and Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Following this time period where you were in Travnik and Kiseljak, where did you go next in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I was out of Bosnia. I was in other parts of former Yugoslavia. I returned in the summer of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And to which part of Bosnia did you return in the summer of 1993?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Initially Central Bosnia again, but only briefly because there were other pressing matters to see to around Mostar and Eastern Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Before turning our attention to Mostar, can you briefly tell us what changes, if any, you'd noticed in Central Bosnia in the summer of 1993 compared to when you had spent time there in January of 1993 or in the autumn of 1992.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Compared to the autumn of 1992, the Lasva Valley, for a start, had completely transformed because the road from Kiseljak to the Vitez junction had already by January become a jigsaw of roadblocks, HVO, HVO, BH, HVO again, with each army staking out, as it were, chunks of road, mostly HVO, and then BH as you got towards Travnik and certainly if you turned right towards Zenica. And then a lot of the houses along that road had been burned out in what was by now a sort of tit-for-tat ethnic cleansing by both sides. And in July, the -- I mean the -- the amount of damage was far more extensive to the point at which I think the road was almost, almost uninhabited. Gornji Vakuf had become a battlefield with the front line going right -- the front line was the main road. Again, one couldn't go through unless one had a armoured vehicle, which I didn't. I had to hitch a ride. But the situation in Central Bosnia had deteriorated into -- I mean, apart from -- sorry, the one difference that had happened is that -- while I was away, is that when I was in Travnik in January, I spent a lot of time with the commander of the HVO, Filipovic, who had gone out of his way to stage a sort of public relations exercise on Mt. Vlasic in which he took a risk to himself and us, I may say, and others with the Bosnian army commander, his counterpart, a man called Kulilovic, up to the Serbian guns together to demonstrate their joint plans to take this post, this antenna together. He talked about, again rather like one of his predecessors, about pressures on him. He said he was walking the edge of a knife, he didn't want the alliance to rupture. By the time I came back, he had gone. In fact, I think the HVO had been -- had been seen out of Travnik by then. I think they'd retreated from Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, I'd like to now turn to Mostar. You indicated a few moments ago in July, 1993, you left Central Bosnia and went to Mostar. Can you tell us, sir, on this occasion approximately how long you remained in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I didn't go to Mostar in July, 1993. I went to Grude to try to get to Mostar in 1993. The -- there had been since May reports of serious fighting within Mostar between the armija BH and the HVO, and by July what became later known as the siege of East Mostar was effectively mounted. I went to Grude to try and get permission or to get some kind of -- find out if there was, you know, a way into East Mostar to what was by then a surrounded pocket effectively under siege by the HVO on three sides and the Serbs to the east, but the permission -- the request was declined. The other reports we heard were about violence and events in Capljina and Stolac, so we asked if we could go to Capljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, before -- before we discuss this request to go to Capljina, let me ask you, why was it necessary to get permission to go into Mostar in July, 1993?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I think you still needed permission to go into West Mostar, because there was a war going on there. I don't know about that. Our interest was to try and into East Mostar because, as I say, it was effectively cut off and under siege. Well, you couldn't get anywhere near the place without going through large numbers of HVO checkpoints, and I imagine that papers would be necessary. As it turned out, I don't think anybody had got into East Mostar and wasn't going to for a long time. In fact, I can remember a spokesman for Mr. Boban, who declined to see us on that occasion, if he was informed, but we were told he wouldn't see us, said that -- I think -- yes, I remember him saying no one's going to get there for two months, and he was almost right, as it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, let's return, then, to this instance where you requested permission to go to Capljina. Do you recall the approximate date when you made this request and to whom?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: The request was made to a Canadian spokesman for Mate Boban, whose name was George. I don't have a surname, I'm afraid. He'll just have to be called George the Canadian. Date, this is -- it must be mid-July. Again, I'm sorry about these dates. They're traceable because of what I wrote. And if I -- if I had a date for an article, I could then work out the exact date, but we're, I think, middle to back end of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Again, 1993?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: 1993 for sure, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And George the Canadian, what -- did George the Canadian speak Serbo-Croatian?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, he did, but we spoke to him in English. I mean, he was from Canada.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And where did you have this discussion with George the Canadian?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: This was at Mate Boban's new headquarters. He'd moved again. Still in Grude but now somewhere on the outskirts in a sort of -- I think it must be an industrial complex. He had a much bigger, bigger premises.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you relate to us what the conversation was that you had with George the Canadian.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: We wanted to go to Capljina because I heard -- had heard that -- there were reports that Muslim men were being taken missing from Capljina and Stolac and that Capljina was the worst and we wanted to get there, and George said no, we couldn't because it's an action zone, a military action zone, I think he even said. And I retorted that that's absurd, it's far away from any kind of front line. And he said you can't go anyway, which made one obviously all the more inclined to go, because that means they've got something to hide, which they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And how long did this discussion with George the Canadian last on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I think it was fairly long because there was a lot of -- because there was the Mostar -- Mostar request, but he didn't -- he did leave us for a bit, went back. An hour or so perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And following this discussion, what steps, if any, did you take?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: We took steps to try to get to Capljina, and we were turned back, and then we had an idea that the translator -- I was working with a man from the Washington Post. The translator lived nearby so instead of using the Washington Post car, we went and got his beat-up old car and he drove and my journalist colleague and I just sort of lounged around in the back. I remember spitting out of the window, reading a newspaper I didn't understand. I think my colleague put his feet out of the window and we got waved through. The car had Croatian plates.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately where this checkpoint was that you got waved through?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: It was quite close to Capljina because we -- there wasn't -- there wasn't a long drive between the checkpoint and the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you describe for the Trial Chamber what you saw when you arrived in the town of Capljina on that day.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. It was a different sort of menacing atmosphere. The streets had very few civilians on them, a few soldiers, not many. There was selective damage. What I've described in Prozor was not the case. But we first asked an old man about these reports that the -- that -- what had been going on, and he said his son had been taken away. A woman we spoke to, I can't remember what she said, but she said go to the mosque, so we did. It seemed like a good idea. The mosque, by the way, was standing, and as I recall, unharmed. The imam was there, so we didn't have a Prozor on our hands but we had another -- another very distressing situation. There were women with the imam, and other women joined him and us as we talked, and the pattern was -- well, because of what I'd been doing up in other parts of Bosnia around Prijedor, was spine chilling because the men had been, it seemed, over the past -- let's see, I do remember them saying it started on the 4th of July because that's a date one remembers. So I remember thinking it's about 10 days. So we're probably 12th 13th-ish July, to try and answer your previous question. The men had been apprehended. One woman told us about how her husband or son had been apprehended while practising football, but what astonished me was that another woman said that her husband had actually been taken - or son, I forget which - on the front lines themselves. In this area, there was no effective Bosnian army. The HVO was the only militia that -- or army that would -- would have been fighting against the Serbs on a front towards the east, and the Muslims would have joined that. I'd come to know a lot about the ethos of the front line and the collegiality of the front line by now and the way that soldiers who fight together think and bond and suffer together and laugh together, and to me it was astonishing, this notion that men in the HVO were being arrested by men in the HVO, having fought together. So I thought this is -- this is -- this is a very important story. But the even more important story was where have they gone? And these women said that they'd gone to camps, and they gave us two names and the names were Dretelj and Gabela. And Gabela was actually on a map. It's near the Croatian border. Dretelj I couldn't find on my map. And we left shortly after this conversation. The imam did talk. I don't remember much about what he said. I must have written it somewhere. And we returned as a matter of urgency on hearing about this word -- hearing this word "camps," which sent a shiver up my spine, to Grude.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, let me ask you a couple of follow-on questions to what you've just told us. Do you recall, sir, the name of the imam in Capljina that you met with on at that day?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Palic, but I don't remember his first name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you remember, sir, if prior to this day you had ever heard of Dretelj or Gabela?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: No, I don't -- no, I hadn't. We -- as I testified earlier, I did not know at that point that I had been to the place the name of which I'd just heard. I had not heard of Dretelj. It just so happens -- I found out another time, later, that I had been there but I hadn't heard the name, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, when I interrupted you, you told us you had gone back to Grude upon hearing the word "camps." Can you tell us approximately what time you arrived back in Grude on this day in mid-July, 1993?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: It would have been late afternoon, early evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you have any meetings or discussions with anyone in Grude when you arrived back in late afternoon, early evening?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, Canadian George again. And we wanted to ask him about Capljina and what had happened there. I omitted some of the other unpleasant things we wanted to talk about. The treatment of women was particularly unpleasant, apparently. A woman tried to hide some valuables inside her underwear and said shamefacedly that they had found it. We wanted to talk about Capljina, but most of all we wanted to ask him where these men had gone, that we'd heard the names Dretelj and Gabela and we wanted to go there, and he said no. But he did know what we were talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And when you --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: He also said you can't have been to Capljina because we didn't give you permission. We said, well, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And what was his reaction at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: He was visibly, visibly not necessarily angry, but I think unnerved because he knew we weren't supposed to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And how long did you have a discussion with Canadian George on the late afternoon on this day?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Well, with hindsight, it probably should have been longer, we should have pushed harder on Dretelj, but it can't have been more than 20 minutes or so because we ended up, I think, that night at Medjugorje before dark, so it would have been half hour or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Why did you go to Medjugorje on that day?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: On that day why did you go to Medjugorje?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Because it was place to stay. But there was also a UNHCR mission in Medjugorje, a United Nations High Commission for Refugees. And in my experience although camps and prisoner registration is the business of the International Committee of the Red Cross, the UNHCR was often a more profitable, at least, source to talk to. So we went in pursuit of the UNHCR office where it so happened that two English speaking people worked, American and/or Australian, I can't remember. I may have written their names in an article, but I can't remember them now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, did you speak to these two English-speaking people --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: -- that day?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: -- at length.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall or can you recount for us the topics of conversation?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, the existence of these camps Dretelj and Gabela, which the existence of which they confirmed, they had heard of these places, and they added a third, called Rodoch, or Rodoc, which was some sort of Heliodrom near Mostar. They said that they had tried to get access and been refused, as had the ICRC. We also talked about the man who -- whose name we'd heard in Capljina, the mayor, and who we had attempted to see but who either wasn't there, as we were told, or didn't want to see us. His name was Markovic. And we actually had quite a long conversation about Markovic and his views. He was described as very extreme by the UNHCR. And then we had a third sort of bit of the conversation which was perhaps the most interesting and alarming. The two people whose names I could probably get, and indeed might have written, told us about a meeting that they had had with local Bosnian Croat authorities and the foreign minister of Croatia proper, a man called Granic, Mate Granic, and they had been invited to this meeting to discuss the possibility of mass deportation of some 50.000 people, men, from this area through a transit camp in -- I think it was intended to be in Ljubuski, where I had actually visited, another internment place, to third-party countries. An astonishing but horribly familiar piece of blackmail, because the people like the UNHCR had been put in a similar position in north-western Bosnia by the Bosnian Serbs, namely that you either cooperate in the grotesque process of ethnic cleansing or you don't and the men remain festering in camps. We had come across that before and here -- here they were -- here was the UNHCR talking about this dilemma again. They had said that they would not cooperate. But I think they reported Mr. -- Minister Granic as saying that the government in Croatia was prepared to cooperate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall, Mr. Vulliamy, any of the specifics that were related to you by the UNHCR people concerning when and where this meeting had taken place?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I think it was Makarska, on the coast, but I may be wrong. I think it was Makarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you have any recollection of when that meeting had been held?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't, no. But I had been given to understand by the women in Capljina, and I'm thinking -- I'm thinking -- I'm improvising here, the women in Capljina had said that the roundup had begun on July the 4th. I remember the date for obvious reasons. Nothing to do with the war, of course. And so I suppose it must have been fairly recently, but I don't remember them telling us when it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, on page 80, lines 24, 25, and into the first line of page 81, you indicated that the UNHCR people confirmed Dretelj and Gabela?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And told you about a place Rodoc. You said, "They said that they had tried to get access but were refused, as had the ICRC." Do you know which of those three locations they were referring to when they said they had been denied access?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I don't, I'm afraid, and I'm not sure they specified. If they did, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned a person by the name of Markovic. Can you recall any of the specifics about what you discussed concerning this person?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, it was a conversation -- I mean, the tenor of the conversation was almost of sick humour. The man of the two who was American talked about a document that apparently Markovic had issued or that he'd seen but did not have in Capljina. I'm talking about a breeding programme for the Muslims whose womenfolk were to be refused entry into maternity hospitals because they tended to breed -- I can't remember the exact words but something about anti-authoritarian individuals. I mean, vile stuff. But I hasten to say I didn't see the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: During July, 1993, did you remain in Bosnia throughout that entire month?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: No. No. I left because by this time I was in discussions about having to write a book and to write it fairly quickly. And I did leave to at least begin writing this thing. I have to say pretty dissatisfied with myself that we'd failed to get into Dretelj and failed to get into East Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: When you say, sir, that you were in discussions to write a book, did those discussions come to fruition?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. They wanted to -- they wanted it before the autumn. That's why I left, to start trying to organise this thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And when you say you left, to what location did you go?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Great Britain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How long did you remain in Great Britain?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Not as long as I'd planned because, well, two things happened during August. The first was that a colleague of mine, Maggie O'Cane, wrote a story for my paper about the first prisoners being released from -- now, I think it was Gabela and Rodoc, but I'm not sure, but that can be checked in the article. The report was that by "release" they meant making men run naked across territory towards Jablanica while they fired guns over their heads. So that was -- you know, I felt that the camp story was about to move and that whatever work I was work -- doing would not be up-to-date unless I went back. But more importantly, or at least I thought at the time, a man from the BBC had finally got into East Mostar, as had the first aid convoys, and this was now a calamitous situation. His report was unforgettable and clearly my work on this book was not going to be up-to-date until I had got into East Mostar and tried again to get into Dretelj, Gabela, or Rodoc.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, what steps, if any, did you take at that point in time to try to get to these locations?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Well, my intention had been to make East Mostar the priority because it was so much in the news, although I'm not sure many people were getting in yet, many other people. But the plan changed because a letter appeared -- soon after arriving in Split, if not that day or the day after, a letter and an article appeared in a newspaper which I recall as being Slobodna Dalmacija, and it was a letter from President Franjo Tudjman to Mate Boban about the camps, and I forget the -- the actual wording, but it was all about complying with international law, complying with the Geneva Conventions, and I think I should explain that the backdrop to this is that by now there was talk of sanctions against Croatia, particularly from the Americans and the British unless something was done, or at least pressure was put on by Zagreb to ameliorate the situation in the camps and with regard to the siege of East Mostar and other matters. And anyway, in a very unusual move, President Tudjman --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I hate to object at this point and interrupt. I've been waiting patiently, but all this afternoon we've heard a lot of speculation, a lot of reading into events, and now the gentleman here is about to do the same thing, and I've been waiting patiently. He's very colourful, wonderful usage of the English language, but I don't think this is proper testimony. If he has specific information, he can give it to us. There may be other witnesses that might be able to tell us what exactly President Franjo Tudjman had in mind when he issued this letter, but now we're going to -- way into speculation. Perhaps historians can write about it but I don't think this is proper testimony from this particular witness unless a proper foundation can be laid, and I dare say one has not been laid for this sort of speculation at this point in time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The objection stands. This letter from Tudjman, is it a letter that the witness has seen or read? Because we are now entering into pure speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I can explain a little bit about this, either in the presence of the witness or we can ask the witness to leave the courtroom. I believe, however, the witness was about to get to that point at the -- shortly after -- or would have gotten to that point shortly after my learned colleague objected.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I have no problems with having a conversation, for the record, outside the presence of the witness. I'm not suggesting that he may not be able to have some information, but I haven't heard a foundation at this point in time. There's one thing: The letter. He might have written -- read the letter or read the article, but now we're going into a psychoanalysis as to what exactly was motivating President Tudjman, and so on and so forth. If they want to lay out the foundation and then the Trial Chamber can draw whatever conclusions it wishes, that's fine. But here now he's delving into -- delving into President Tudjman's psyche as to what motivated him at this particular point in time, and he's done this over and over again. I haven't objected, but at this point I think this is a little bit -- way too much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Again, Mr. President, very, very briefly in the presence of the witness, what we'll say is that he's laying out the context in which this article appeared and when he saw this -- or what he will testify about this material, he's simply putting it into a context of other events that were going on at that time, and that's precisely what the witness was explaining at the point when the objection occurred. And again if you take a look at lines 18 through 24 of page 84, you will see that the witness was explaining the context in which this article appeared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll take up this question myself. Sir, you mentioned a letter from President Tudjman. My question is a very simple one: If you are familiar with this letter, did you include the contents of the letter in an article drafted by yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the letter was read to me in translation. I've since seen it in English but not at the time it was read to me in translation, and I only mentioned it because it changed our plans and priorities and -- and was a reason to attempt, as soon as possible - in fact at that day - to get access to one of these camps. It had currency. Did I quote it? I certainly referred to it. I probably quoted it, but I'm afraid I can't answer you, Your Honour. It was -- I just don't remember the specific article, but it would certainly have been referred to in the article, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you are saying that someone translated this letter for you, and the translation of the letter is the reason for which you decided that you should go and visit the camps. Is that what you are telling us now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, because quite apart from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who translated this letter for you, and how is it that this person came to know about the letter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The letter was in a newspaper called Slobodna Dalmacija, which -- which we read almost every day we could. And the person who translated it was a correspondent for a newspaper, The Daily Telegraph, who had lived many years in Belgrade and read and spoke the language fluently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which means that given the contents of the letter, you as a journalist decided to examine the issue of the camps. That's correct, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To return -- to return to the issue of the camps which had now become almost a diplomatic matter as well as a humanitarian one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness Vulliamy, do you recall the substance of the letter that was translated to you by your colleague from The Daily Telegraph?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: In essence, it was a -- an urging from President Tudjman to Mate Boban to ensure that conditions in the camps be brought within international law and -- and within the Geneva Convention.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, you mentioned at page 86, line 23 and 24, "I've since seen it in English." Do you recall when you saw it in English?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: On Sunday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: On do you recall the format in which you saw the letter in English?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: It was in a -- in a press release, as I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Or attached to a press release.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And the document that you saw on Sunday, who showed you that document?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: One of your colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And did you have an opportunity to read that document?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did that document, to the best of your recollection, reflect the material that was published in Slobodna Dalmacija in 1993?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I -- I -- I mean, all -- no reason to suppose that it wasn't the same letter. I mean, it ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And again, what was the contents of that letter that you saw on Sunday?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Well, a -- an urging to Mate Boban to ensure that the camps were within the international law and comply with the Geneva Convention.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd ask that the witness be shown what's been marked as P9497, and we do have this in e-court. If we could please -- if we could please go, on the English version, to page 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, do you see a document in front you on the screen?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, in Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: In Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Could we have that perhaps, for the benefit of the witness ... If we could please go to page 5 of this document. Mr. President, it appears that page 5 is not --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, do you now see a document before you in English?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, is this the document that you were shown on Sunday?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, it is. As -- and the press release is the cover. It's -- it's a continuation. It's attached to that, stapled to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And you had an opportunity to read this document on Sunday?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vulliamy. I'd like to return now to the events that you were discussing for us. Do you recall approximately the date at which your colleague read this letter that was published in Slobodna Dalmacija to you?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I think it's the 20th -- where are we? No, I don't. I can't give you an exact date, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the month and year?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: It's certainly September, and it's certainly 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you at that point in time, sir, see the article in Slobodna Dalmacija?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Oh, yes. We had it in Split.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you, sir, what steps, if any, you took in September, 1993, to visit any of the camps that we were discussing a few moments ago; that is, Dretelj, Gabela, or Rodoc.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: We drove straight to Grude to find -- or to try and meet Mate Boban and ask him if we could go. Dretelj was the one that I think we chose. I think the UNHCR had said it was the one they were most worried about, and it was the one we tried last time so why not try again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you have any discussions with anyone at Grude concerning entry to this camp?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. Canadian George again. And we asked to see Mate Boban. I'm not sure he was there when we got there about late morning. We were told to come back that afternoon, and Canadian George then said, "No, you can't go to Dretelj."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the approximate date or -- and time that you had this discussion with Canadian George?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: The last one was during the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And the approximate time period in terms of dates; month, year?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: This is September, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, what --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I think we're in early -- early-ish September, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What steps did you take after you were told by Canadian George that you can't go to Dretelj?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: We decided that this was pressing matter now and we stayed in Grude and thought that we'd try again the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you in fact try again the following day?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Same place, back to Mr. Boban's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Who did you encounter on that day?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Well, we met Canadian George again first. He -- I think maybe he did go to ask Mate Boban if we could go to Dretelj, and we were -- I think he told us no again and we asked him to go and try again. We were sitting in an office attached to this complex, whatever it was, I don't know what it was, on the outskirts of Grude, and then somebody came into the room or passed us whom all three of us recognised although it wasn't me who recognised him first, and it was one of my two colleagues, I think from the BBC. He said, Oh, there's General Praljak, why don't we ask him?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And what happened next?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: We did ask him. And I can't remember exactly whether he left us for a while. I think he did and came back but not that long afterwards, and said, I have to say to my surprise, Yes, so far as I'm concerned, you can. Or I paraphrase those words. I wasn't taking notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And after this discussion with General Praljak, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: An order paper, "odobrenje," was drawn up. I honestly don't recall whether General Praljak returned into the room with it or whether it was typed up. I think it was typed up in our presence. It was stamped and signed, and with surprisingly little ado, and I don't think we talked to General Praljak very much after that. We set off to Dretelj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How did you know where to go?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Our translator guide knew where to go. And it was -- it was towards Capljina. I think by then we'd found it on the map, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: This document that you were provided with, whose signature appeared on it?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, it was General Praljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please describe for us what you did after you set off for Dretelj.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: We got there, and -- yes, I think the translator did know where to go. Well, for me it was very strange, because it was -- you know, I'd been there before, and I said to my colleagues, I've been here before. As I said, I didn't know the name of the place. So far as I was concerned, it was called Capljina, for Serbian prisoners. And we presented our paper to a visibly surprised guard who then disappeared to a building behind the gate. The gate remained shut and we were told to wait.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What was this guard wearing?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: HVO uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How long did you wait?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
