utterances.text: I think about 20 minutes to half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And approximately what time of day was it?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: This would be late morning, mid to late morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us what happened after the guard returned?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I don't remember whether he returned with the commander of the camp or whether he brought us in to a sort of office block where the commander of the camp was - I think it was the latter - but we were introduced. He was cordial but, I think, surprised. I didn't get the impression that any forward call had been made from Grude to tell him of our -- that we were coming. And as I say, it was all very sudden.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the name of this person who was the commander of the camp?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Shakota or Sakota.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: We had initial discussion, which I don't recall very much of. We were anxious to get on because we were now in. And we began a tour of the camp, after he'd outlined various, as it were, rules of operation, rules of engagement for interviews, which were that he would be -- he would have to be -- he wanted to be present at them and that they would be done through the translator and that we weren't supposed to speak to the prisoners out of his earshot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How many of you were with your group?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: It was translator, whose name I'm afraid I don't have, a woman called Cathy Evans from the BBC, Mike Montgomery from The Daily Telegraph, of London, and a man called John Landy from a news organisation in America called Knight Ridder.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And who accompanied you as you entered the Dretelj camp?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: As we went from the administrative block for the tour, if that's the right word, Commander Sakota himself -- if it's Sakota. I'm sorry, I can't remember which it was. And a couple of armed guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Could you please describe for the Trial Chamber what you observed as you went into the camp from the administrative block.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: The first port of call was a medical facility, a small to medium sized building with beds, military-style iron beds, quite tight -- quite closely -- I wouldn't say packed, quite closely organised so that the doctors could only just pass through between them. Two to a bed, dirty blankets, dirty mattresses, very, very hot, and we began -- well, the men -- they were all men, were in varying states. They were skin very, very dry, skin problems, they looked malnourished, vacant stares. It was a distressing sight.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Approximately how many men were in this medical facility, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Again, I -- I -- I don't like making these estimates. Perhaps 20, 25. Of that order, but it could have been less, it could have been more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you have any discussions with any of the persons who were in this medical facility?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: If we did, they were pretty cursory because the men were not really in a -- in a fit condition to talk very much. But we did talk to one or more of the three doctors who were tending to them, and they were, as is always the system in these camps, they were themselves prisoners who happened to be of the medical profession.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us where you went after the medical facility?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: We went up past -- forgive me if I refer back to the previous visit. Up past a shed on the right where the women had been to a part of the camp, and I now realise that the HOS hadn't showed us -- well, they showed us very little, never mind the women, because we started to go up past an area that I -- we later came back to where some men were eating, to turning right to two hangars, two sort of tunnels like aircraft hangars or bomb shelter-type places dug into two hills opposite, with the entrances opposite each other, two mounds. We headed up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And as you went along this -- these buildings that you've described for us, did you see any people?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Well, guards. I don't -- I mean, yes, there was -- well, there was another building to the left where there were prisoners and a sliding door half open or a third open, but we didn't go in there. We went -- we went up to these tunnels.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And what did you do when you arrived up by the tunnels?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Well, it was -- it was quite a shocking thing to find, because the doors were open but the tunnels were -- well, I won't say packed, but there were a lot of men in each one, and -- oh, sorry. Just a second. I've actually left out the -- we did go into the -- to the shed on the right where the women had been in 1992. Forgive me. We did that before we went to the tunnels.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well, what did you see, sir? What did you see in the building where the women had been in in 1992?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Right. In there were prisoners either sitting -- for the most part sitting or crouching on the floor with not much space between them, with their -- I mean, sufficiently little space between them so that they -- if they had any belongings with them, they hung them in plastic bags from rafters across the top of the shed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you speak with any of the people that were in this building?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, we spoke to a number of those because I don't actually remember where the commander was at this point, but the -- the translator was doing some interviews. Mike spoke the language, Cathy spoke some German, I think, which she used. I found a DJ, a disk jockey who spoke some quite good English. We agreed -- we had whispered out on the tarmac that we would share stuff if we split up and talked privately to people. I found somebody who spoke good English from -- I think he was from Stolac, and he told me that things had been much worse in July, he said. The doors of this thing had been shut. They had been shut in for some 72 hours at one point if not repetitively. I was struck by him saying that they had had to get their excretion out of -- throw their excretion out of a window because of the stench and they'd had to drink their own urine to hydrate themselves during those periods that the doors were kept tight shut. I don't remember what he said about feeding during that times, those 72-hour periods, but my inference was that they were not fed. This wasn't recent to our visit, this was back in July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you now, sir, go forward to the point in time where you went to the structures you described as the tunnels and tell us what you saw there.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. Forgive me, Your Honours, for leaving out that important detail. When we got to the tunnels, this was, you know, the most distressing bit, because these men were -- were in these tunnels. The doors were open but they were still quite dark at the back. And although the doors were open, as I recall, the commander stayed outside as did the guards, and -- although one or two guards might have come in. I went into the first, into the one on my right, which I think makes it the southernmost, I'm not sure of the directions, and started to talk actually through the translator but unsupervised at first and then joined my colleague who spoke Serbo-Croat who was talking to some other people and translated and we began to talk to the prisoners in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, what, if anything, can you recall about your discussions that you had with the prisoners who were in the tunnel?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Well, I recall what they looked like first of all. They were in -- in bad condition. They were pale. They had -- their eyes were watery. There was no sign of beating, I have to say, although someone at some point said someone had been killed with a plank of wood not so long ago, but they showed signs of extreme, extreme neglect in terms of nutrition, hydration, skin and such. They talked again about July. They mentioned one particular episode when the guards had got drunk outside and were singing songs and opened fire through the doors and against this hangar, this tunnel, and they told us that bullets had come through the doors and that people had been killed. To back up that narrative, there were pockmarks on the back wall, and there were also piercings in the doors, in the metal doors with metal gnarled inwards to indicate a shot. They told me that people had died that night. They also talked about conditions. Again, they said that back in July, those -- even those doors had been shut for 72 hours, for 72-hour periods, with so far as I can remember with, this time, no windows through which excretia could be got rid of, and again they repeated that they needed to drink their own urine in order to hydrate. It was an appalling narrative.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, did you ask anyone why they had been locked into these rooms for 72 hours?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I think one of my colleagues might have done. And -- and -- but this is a conversation I would have had later, that it might have coincided with military events outside, perhaps an advance by the Bosnian army or something. But what we did ask was about what had happened recently since Commander Sakota had arrived, and there was some dispute between the inmates about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, I know you've told us several times you dislike numbers, but can you give us a rough approximation as to how many people were in either these two tunnels or in one of those tunnels?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Three figures apiece, I'd say. Low hundreds. We did actually ask Commander Sakota how many men were in the camp, and he gave us a figure around 1.400. The UNHCR later informed us that the number had been very much higher earlier in the summer. Inside those tunnels, I'd say low hundreds in each. I --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And in the shed, the first building that you entered, how many --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: The one on the right, with the plastic bags hanging.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: More. Again -- again must have been hundreds. And as I say we passed another building on the left that we didn't go into that was less full, actually. Say scores for that one. In the back of my mind there's a figure of 1.400. I had no reason to disbelieve Commander Sakota, but I would say low hundreds, but warily.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, you told us that many of these people appeared to be malnourished. Did you ask anyone about nourishment that they received?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I don't think we did ask people about nourishment, although back in the medical facility, if that's the right word for it, which it probably isn't, the doctor did say that along with treating broken ribs - I think you can probably work out what that means - he did indicate that some men had died from what he called natural causes, and made a gesture like this and like that which suggested either -- I mean heat and lack of food and/or water.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: In total, Mr. Vulliamy, how long did you remain in Dretelj on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Probably about two hours if not a little more, because we were talking periodically with the commander as we made the tour. And some of these conversations went on quite a long time. I mean, there was an incident when one man actually got up, gave his name and origin and wanted to say that since Commander Sakota arrived, things had got much better. And there was a lot of hissing and booing going on. We also wanted to find out about the ICRC, the Red Cross visit, and there was quite a long conversation about that, both with the commander and with the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, during the two hours if not a little more that you were in the camp, what did you observe the detainees doing?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Well, I mean nothing, and that's the point really. I think one of the things that struck me was that although these doors of the hangars were now open and it was a hot, sunny day, a lot of the prisoners, inmates in the tunnels, just wanted to remain in the tunnels if not sit up against the back wall. They -- they were doing nothing. I presumed, actually, whether the doors were opened regularly or for our benefit I don't -- I don't know, but I presume that there was a daily opening of these doors, but what interested me was that none of them seemed to want to go outside despite the opportunity for -- for some fresh air. I didn't take heart from that. You know, I thought it showed signs of either fear of going out or -- or something. And indeed one prisoner did say, "We're not really allowed out anyway. It's too frightening to go outside."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you observe any prisoners outside?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, oh, yes, yes. A few went out to hang about outside the tunnels. And by the time we came back down the very gentle slope from the tunnels, there was a mealtime going on at the top of a sort of track, where some grass is on a corner.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you describe for us what this mealtime looked like to you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, and I'd seen similar in other places. It was a sort of drill of refreshment and humiliation at the same time. You line up in organised groups and, marshalled by men with guns, you jog, in this case, from the shed where the women were before, as I said where the plastic bags were, over for your meal. In this case it was eaten in complete silence as regards us because -- I don't know. They were eating and I didn't want to interrupt them, but there were guards around, anyway, with guns, and they -- and I have reason from previous experience to be wary of -- of this -- of the consequences of talking to people in these circumstances, and -- but they were sort of -- I don't know whether they were made or wanted to but they were sort of crouching and eating a meal -- a meal of watery stew which had been cooked outside, in fact, and then they would finish and return to their quarters and be replaced by another shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, do you remember any of the topics that you discussed with these detainees?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Well, we asked who they were, and some of them were civilians. A lot of them had been members of the HVO. They'd been fighting. They had been fighting with the -- with the people who -- for the organisation which was incarcerating them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What ethnicity were these people?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you ask them what geographic areas they were from?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. They came from Stolac, Capljina - which answered the question from July, Where have the men gone? - the villages around the area, and a few were from Mostar. One young boy was from Sarajevo, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you ask any of the detainees how long they'd been there?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I didn't, but they all -- or at least I don't recall having done so. Some looked as if they'd come more recently than others, for sure. They were in better condition than others. Yet others were talking about sufferings that they -- that they recalled from July, early to mid-July. So they'd been there -- to look at them I think different lengths of time but some had been there from the early weeks of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, you referred on page 101, line 16, to a young boy from Sarajevo. Do you have idea approximately how old this person was?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: When I say "young boy," I don't mean a child. He was a teenager, maybe 14, 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you ask any of the detainees if they had had any visitors?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Well, we talked about the visit of the International Committee of the Red Cross, and we talked about that with Commander Sakota as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What was the discussion? What was the subject of the discussion concerning the visit of the International Committee of the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Well, they were very different. Commander Sakota told us they'd been - I think they'd been the previous day, or the day that we'd first asked to go into the camp, and -- and Commander Sakota, who -- who implied that he did -- in his body language, his language, in fact, he did not actually enjoy this job he had, to be honest, told us that he'd got a phone call from again the Croatian Foreign Minister Mate Granic sometime previous to the ICRC visit, asking him to ameliorate the conditions in the camp, and he told us that, and -- and he did say something which I wish I could remember, but it was, you know, something to the effect that he would actually quite like all these people just to be able to go home. The discourse with the prisoners about the visit of the ICRC was very different. I have no way of corroborating this, but some of them, two of them in particular back in the tunnels, said that 120 men in -- in the worst condition in the camp had been removed before the ICRC arrived. I don't know whether that's true or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, did you meet with an investigator or an analyst of this Tribunal in 1997?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And did you give a statement at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you attach anything to your statement?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: If this is the statement that I gave during the trial of Colonel, later General, Blaskic, yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What did you attach --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Two -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What did you --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Two drawings of the -- a very rough recollection of the layout of Dretelj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd ask the witness be shown these two sketches prior to recessing for the evening. The first one has been marked as P8761.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, do you see a document or a sketch in front of you?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us what that is?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: It's -- it's -- yes, it's my attempt to recreate the layout of the places I went to in Dretelj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And again, do you recall the approximate date that you made this sketch?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: It would be, I suppose, 1997 -- springtime, 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would ask that the witness now be shown 8762, P8762.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document, Mr. Vulliamy?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, I do. This is my attempt, I presume on the same day, to give a sort of elevation of how the two tunnels, as we've called them, were dug into the mounds, into the hills.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And towards the bottom on the right-hand side, can you describe for us what you were attempting to draw.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, that's an attempt to again give a sort of dissection of how the -- the -- the bullet holes, as it says, in the doors, gnarled inwards to support the narrative that there'd been that shooting that night when the men were locked into the camp after the -- after the booze-up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vulliamy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I note the time. The next thing we'll be doing is showing the witness some photographs and clearly, given the late hour, it would perhaps be best to recess now and resume in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How much time do you need tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe that at this point we're just under three hours in terms of the direct examination. We had indicated a revised estimate of about four hours for the direct examination. I anticipate about one hour remaining, perhaps a little bit more than that, but I certainly would expect that by the first break tomorrow we would be complete with the direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I will ask our legal officer to count the exact amount of time. It seems to me that it's been more than three hours, however, we'll verify this. We shall resume tomorrow. It's almost 7.00 p.m. Thank you, everyone, we continue tomorrow at 9.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honours. Under the Court's decision of earlier today, Mr. Stojic's Defence team will be the first to cross-examine this witness. In listening to the witness's testimony today, it has become clear that he must have transmitted to the Guardian newspaper material which resulted in a considerable number of published articles during the period between August 19 -- or earlier in 1992 and September, 1993. I am, as Your Honour knows, fairly new in this case, but I checked with colleagues, and I believe that these articles have not been the subject of any disclosure from the Prosecution. Your Honour, it seems to me that -- and Mr. Karnavas also mentions that there may be handwritten notes of some -- some relevance. Your Honour, I can't imagine that it would be difficult to obtain these materials if a phone call were to be placed to London to the Guardian newspaper, and it seems to me that this is material that should be provided to the Defence, and I would ask the Prosecution to make an effort to obtain these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Mundis. Have you disclosed to the Defence all the articles written by the witness, all the articles that you have, or is it, as the Defence has said, that you have only disclosed some of the witness's articles written as a journalist in the field? What can you tell us about this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President and Your Honours. We have disclosed those articles which are in our possession. The remainder of the articles are, as would be the case with all the articles, are open-source material. We do not go out and search for material for the purpose of disclosing it to the Defence. Those articles during the course of our work we have come across or downloaded or printed out, my understanding is those have been disclosed, but again, everything else which is in the public domain we do not actively search for for the purpose of downloading or researching the material in order to provide it to the Defence. With respect to the notebooks, that's a subject which the witness could be asked about, and we will certainly be doing that tomorrow morning prior to his testimony, but if Your Honours would like, we could very briefly explore that issue with the witness right now so that this issue can be explained to everyone. I believe the witness has testified about this in prior cases and I would believe that the Defence probably know the story about the notebooks, but we can certainly ask the witness about that at this point, if that would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Put some very brief questions to the witness with regard to the notebooks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, you've heard the discussion that's happened here today. I know you've testified about this in other cases. Would you please tell the Trial Chamber whether you maintained notebooks; and if so, what has happened to those notebooks?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. Of course I maintained notebooks, and they've been very thoroughly scrutinised and severally photocopied over the years. I don't have them. They were last in -- and I may be -- they may not be now, they were last in possession of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, the witness has just told us that he would not rule out the possibility that these notebooks might be in the hands of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have undertaken a complete search for these notebooks within the Office of the Prosecution. We have not been able to locate these notebooks. I believe some of the notebooks were delivered to the Registry for photocopying and became in fact exhibits in another case. I'm not sure to what extent those are the notebooks that have apparently gone missing. The -- again, I don't want to testify here, but the attorney that Mr. Vulliamy has dealt with in the past concerning the notebooks is no longer with the Office of the Prosecutor, and we simply do not know where the notebooks have gone to the extent that they were in fact delivered to the Office of the Prosecutor. I need to correct something also, Mr. President. My case manager in the last few moments has informed me that we did not in fact disclose any of the articles that have been written by the witness. That's presumably because we don't necessarily have them. Again, open-source material, our position is open-source material which is available to anyone who conducts due diligence in order to find that material, via the internet or other open sources has the ability to do that. So I need to correct what I said earlier about disclosing articles. It turns out we have not in fact done that. But again, with respect to the notebooks, additional questions can be put to the witness concerning the notebooks, and that was certainly the subject we are going to touch on tomorrow morning at the conclusion of the direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, with regard to what the Defence has just said, would it be possible for the Guardian to research -- to carry out some research with regard to the articles that you have published and could those articles be provided, perhaps through the internet, and naturally, if necessary, one could pay to have these articles made available, or would you say this is not a possibility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a possibility in many ways. Noting my watch, Your Honour, what they call the research department of the library shut five minutes ago. The -- but there is a service which I'm sure is -- someone will have access to, called Lexis, where you simply tap in key words and if you tap in my name and Bosnia and choose some dates, you get a list of them all. It's quite a long one. They are publicly available to anyone who can get to the internet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, sir, you have the entire night to gain access to these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, let me just make this observation, if I may: It is the obligation of the Prosecutor under Rule 66(B) to make available documents that are in the Prosecutor's custody or control which are material to the preparation of the Defence, and, Your Honour, where these documents are effectively in the custody of a Prosecution witness, it's my submission that they fall under this provision, and it's not enough to -- for the Prosecutor to refer us to Lexis, a service for -- a commercial service, in order to fulfil its obligations under this Article, and I would respectfully invite the Court to require the Prosecution to make these materials available to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Murphy, if I have understood what Mr. Mundis said correctly, the notebooks were not found, and they cannot thus be disclosed. As far as the articles are concerned, he disclosed the articles that he had, whereas other articles that are open-source articles are articles that everyone could have access to. This is how I have interpreted Mr. Mundis's submission. Mr. Mundis, is this the Prosecution's approach in relation to Rule 66(B) of the Rules of Procedure?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, let me again correct what I said earlier. We did not disclose articles because they are open-source materials. In the event that we have materials or documents which are under our control or are in our custody and which is not open-source material, we will provide that to the Defence. But again, when there is material that is available to anyone exercising due diligence, then we don't believe that it's our obligation to affirmatively go out and obtain information which is publicly available for the purpose of disclosing it to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll leave the matter there, but let me inform the Defence that they have had the witness list for a long time, and this witness was included on the list, this journalist was included on the list. And if one is a Defence lawyer, the least one could do is look into the sort of work that the journalist was involved in, look into the articles drafted by the journalist, and for a number of weeks no one has been able to do this. It's now 7.10. We will resume tomorrow morning at 9.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 9th day of May, 2006, at 9.00 a.m. 21 22 23 24 25
